title: Read a language before solving it
summary: Identify the alphabet, order, counts and boundary cases before building a grammar or machine.
goals: Read set-builder notation aloud.
Distinguish the empty string from the empty language.
Separate order requirements from counting requirements.
Test examples and counterexamples systematically.

sections.title: The complete task
sections.html:
A language is a set of strings. A grammar generates strings in that set; an automaton decides whether an input string belongs to that set. Start with the language itself: what symbols may occur, in what order, and with what relationships between their counts?

For example, L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} contains one block of zeros followed by an equally long block of ones. Examples include ε, 01 and 0011. The string 0101 has equal counts, but its order is wrong.

sections.title: Read each symbol
sections.html:
NotationRead it asExample
ΣThe alphabet: the available symbolsΣ = {0,1}
Σ*All finite strings over Σ, including εε, 0, 1, 00, 01, …
εThe empty string; its length is zero0⁰ = ε
∅The empty set: a language containing no stringsε ∉ ∅
ε ∈ {ε}The empty string belongs to the set containing the empty string{ε} has one element
w ∈ LThe string w is a member of L0011 ∈ L

|w|ₐThe number of occurrences of a in w|abaca|ₐ = 3
wᴿThe reverse of w(001)ᴿ = 100
:Such that{0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}

0ⁿ means n copies of the symbol 0. It is repetition notation, not numerical exponentiation. Unless a language says otherwise, exponents here are nonnegative integers.

sections.title: Keep order and counts separate
sections.html:
0ⁿ1ᵐ imposes the order: first zeros, then ones. A condition such as n = m then constrains the two block lengths. In contrast, {w ∈ {a,b}* : |w|ₐ = |w|ᵦ} permits interleaving. It contains abba, baba and ba.

For several blocks, write a count table before constructing anything. In aⁱbʲcᵏ, the exponents belong to a, b and c respectively. Every inequality must be translated into a specific relationship.

sections.title: Why context-free languages appear
sections.html:
Unbounded nesting, such as balanced parentheses, needs more than the finite memory of a finite automaton. A context-free grammar can generate matching structure recursively. A pushdown automaton adds a stack to recognize such structure.

Every regular language is context-free. Some context-free languages are not regular, such as {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Some languages are not context-free. A pattern that looks like a dependency is a useful design clue, but it is not a test that proves a language context-free.

worked.title: Classify strings in a two-block language
worked.intro: Use L = {aⁱbʲ : i ≥ 1 and j = 2i}. Decide whether aabbbb belongs by checking alphabet, block order and both numeric conditions. We will work through the whole check before you try another string.

steps.title: Read the definition
steps.html: There must be at least one a. All a symbols precede all b symbols. The b block is twice as long as the a block.

steps.title: Check the alphabet and order
steps.html: aabbbb uses only a and b, with no a after the first b. It has the required two-block form.

steps.title: Count and substitute
steps.html: The counts are i = 2 and j = 4. The conditions become 2 ≥ 1 and 4 = 2·2, both true.

steps.title: Test boundary and nearby failures
steps.html: Therefore aabbbb ∈ L. The shortest member is abb. The empty string fails i ≥ 1; aabb fails the ratio; abbabb fails the order even though its total counts have the right ratio.

practice.prompt: For L = {0ⁿ1ᵐ : n < m}, classify ε, 1, 00111 and 01011.
practice.hint: Check order before the inequality. A zero-length block is allowed unless excluded.
practice.solution: ε: no, 0 < 0 is false. 1: yes, n = 0 and m = 1. 00111: yes, 2 < 3. 01011: no, a zero occurs after a one, so it is not a string of the form 0ⁿ1ᵐ.

practice.prompt: Let w = abaca. Find |w|, |w|ₐ, |w|ᵦ and wᴿ. Explain why ε and ∅ cannot be used interchangeably.
practice.hint: Reverse symbol order; do not sort the symbols.
practice.solution: The answers are 5, 3, 1 and acaba. ε is one string of length zero. ∅ is a set with no strings. A machine may accept ε, but it does not read ∅ as an input string.

check.prompt: Does 0101 belong to {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}? Explain the decisive condition.
check.answer: No. It violates the block order.
check.explanation: The zero after the first one breaks the required 0*1* form. Equal counts alone are insufficient.

transfer.prompt: Define a language of three blocks of a, b and c where the first and third blocks are nonempty and equally long, and the middle block can have any length. Give three members and three nonmembers, explaining each failure.
transfer.solution: L = {aⁱbʲcⁱ : i ≥ 1, j ≥ 0}. Members: ac, abc, aabbbcc. Nonmembers: ε (nonempty outer blocks required), aabc (outer counts differ), abac (block order fails).

setup:
A string is a finite sequence of symbols, such as aabbbb. A language is a set of strings. This first lesson asks whether a particular string obeys a definition; no grammar or machine construction is needed yet.

Notation in the first exampleRead it in words
{aⁱbʲ : i ≥ 1 and j = 2i}All strings made of i copies of a followed by j copies of b, such that i is at least 1 and j is twice i.
aⁱbʲWrite all the as first, then all the bs. The superscripts count repetitions; they are not arithmetic powers.
:, ≥, =Such that; at least; equal to. The counts i and j are integers.

For aabbbb, count two as and four bs, then check order and the equation separately. A count of zero means that block is absent. ε names the string with no symbols.

In later shorthand, a* means zero or more as, and a*b* means a block of zero or more as followed by a block of zero or more bs. A concatenation joins strings in order: ab followed by c gives abc.
bridge: Next, a grammar will generate strings rather than simply classify them. Keep the alphabet, order, count conditions and smallest cases visible when you read its rules.

title: Read and run a context-free grammar
summary: Understand the four parts of a CFG and exactly what a production permits.
goals: Identify terminals, variables, productions and the start symbol.
Read alternatives, recursion and epsilon productions.
Apply one production to exactly one variable occurrence.
Distinguish syntax from meaning.

sections.title: A complete grammar first
sections.html:
S → 0S1 | ε

Start with S. Either replace S with 0S1, adding one zero before it and one one after it, or replace S with ε, removing the remaining S. This grammar generates exactly {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}.

The vertical bar means alternative productions. S → 0S1 | ε abbreviates two rules: S → 0S1 and S → ε.

sections.title: The four parts of G = (V, Σ, P, S)
sections.html:
PartMeaningFor this grammar
VVariables, also called nonterminals{S}
ΣTerminals: the actual symbols of output strings{0,1}
PThe production rules{S → 0S1, S → ε}
SThe selected start variableS

V and Σ are disjoint. ε is not a terminal symbol; it denotes a string with no symbols. An ε production is allowed even though ε is not in Σ.

Every production has exactly one variable on the left. Its right side may contain terminals, variables, both, or no symbols. A rule AB → a is not a context-free production because its left side contains two variables.

sections.title: What “context-free” means
sections.html:
If X → ρ is a rule, an occurrence of X may be replaced by ρ regardless of what is immediately before or after it. In αXβ, only the chosen X changes: the result is αρβ.

Do not replace all identical variables at once. With S → SS, the sentential form SS contains two separate occurrences. Replacing the left occurrence using S → a produces aS, not aa.

In this general notation, α, β and ρ (alpha, beta and rho) name whole strings of symbols. They are placeholders for the surrounding parts and replacement, not additional grammar terminals. “Disjoint” in the four-part definition means no symbol is both a variable and a terminal.

sections.title: Tokens, spelling and meaning
sections.html:
In a programming grammar, id represents a token category. cursor and result may both be id tokens, with different lexemes, meaning their actual source text. Punctuation such as (, ), { and , is terminal syntax.

A grammar checks structure. A syntactically valid statement need not make semantic sense: a grammar may generate an expression that refers to an undeclared name. Similarly, an English grammar can generate a grammatical but implausible sentence.

BNF often writes ::= in place of →. Optional or repeated components in extended notation must ultimately be understood as explicit alternatives and recursion.

worked.title: Explain every part of a small list grammar
worked.intro:
Start with the complete supplied grammar and target:

Start variable: S
S → [ L ]
L → ε | id T
T → ε | , id T
Target: [ id , id ]

Each id is one item token. We will apply rules to generate this exact sequence; the square brackets in the grammar are literal terminals, not notation for an optional component.

steps.title: Separate the symbols
steps.html: The variables are S, L and T. The terminals are [, ], id and ,. S is the start symbol.

steps.title: Expand the fixed outside structure
steps.html: S ⇒ [ L ]. The brackets are now fixed terminals; only L can be rewritten.

steps.title: Choose a nonempty list and one additional item
steps.html: [ L ] ⇒ [ id T ] ⇒ [ id , id T ]. The tail rule adds a comma and another id.

steps.title: End the recursion
steps.html: Use T → ε: [ id , id T ] ⇒ [ id , id ]. ε contributes no printed symbol. Using L → ε instead at the earlier point would have generated the empty list [ ].

practice.prompt: For A → aA | b, identify V, Σ, P and the start symbol. Give the shortest member and two longer members.
practice.hint: The variable is a placeholder; the lowercase symbols remain in the output.
practice.solution: V = {A}, Σ = {a,b}, P = {A → aA, A → b}, start A. The shortest member is b; longer examples are ab and aab. The grammar never generates ε because there is no terminating empty production.

practice.prompt: Are X → ε, X → aYX, XY → a and a → X valid CFG productions when X,Y are variables and a is a terminal?
practice.hint: A context-free production must have one variable as its whole left side.
practice.solution: The first two are valid. XY → a has two variables on the left. a → X has a terminal on the left. Neither is a CFG production.

check.prompt: When S → ε is used inside 0S1, what string remains?
check.explanation: Only the occurrence of S is removed. The surrounding terminals remain unchanged.

transfer.prompt:
Use the same grammar from the worked example:

S → [ L ]
L → ε | id T
T → ε | , id T

Here id is one item token. Starting from S, generate [ id , id , id ]. Write the whole string after each replacement, and name the rule you used. Finish with no variables remaining.
transfer.solution:
Start with S. Apply one rule to one variable at each step:

Rule usedWhole string after the replacement
S → [ L ][ L ]
L → id T[ id T ]
T → , id T[ id , id T ]
T → , id T again[ id , id , id T ]
T → ε[ id , id , id ]

The rule L → id T supplies the first item. Each use of T → , id T adds a comma and one more item, leaving a new T that can be replaced again. After three items, T → ε removes only T; the closing bracket stays. The result contains only terminals, so the generation is complete.

setup:
Lesson 1 described which strings belong to a language. A grammar supplies rules that generate them. A variable (or nonterminal) is a symbol that still needs a rule; a terminal is an output symbol that stays as it is. Choose a start variable, then replace one variable occurrence at a time.

SymbolMeaning
S → 0S1A rule: S may be replaced by the three symbols 0, S, 1, in that order.
S → 0S1 | εTwo alternative rules. The vertical bar means “or”; ε replaces S by no symbols.
S ⇒ 0S1One actual replacement using a rule. We use → for rules and ⇒ for steps in a derivation.
idOne terminal token for a name or item. A multi-letter token label still counts as one symbol.

In the list example, S is the whole list, L is its contents, and T is the remaining tail after an item. The brackets and commas are terminals. An empty tail ends the list; it does not erase punctuation already generated. You will read and apply supplied rules here. Grammar design begins in lesson 5.
bridge: Carry forward the difference between a production rule and an actual replacement. Lesson 3 records those replacements as a derivation, keeping the whole current string visible.

title: Build derivations one rule at a time
summary: Turn a target string into an explicit sequence of justified replacements.
goals: Read ⇒ and ⇒* accurately.
Identify a sentential form and a completed derivation.
Construct leftmost and rightmost derivations.
Use the terminal prefix to detect incorrect choices.

sections.title: Derivation, sentential form and membership
sections.html:
A derivation is a sequence of rule applications beginning with the start variable. A sentential form is any string of terminals and variables reached in that sequence. When no variables remain, it is a generated terminal string.

α ⇒ β means one rule application takes α to β. α ⇒* β means zero or more applications. The star includes zero steps: S ⇒* S is true. Membership is defined by L(G) = {w ∈ Σ* : S ⇒* w}.

A derivation proves a particular string belongs. Giving several examples does not prove the grammar generates exactly a proposed language; that stronger statement needs both directions, developed in the grammar-design lesson.

Read the membership definition aloud: the language generated by G is the set of terminal strings w for which some derivation from S produces w. G is the grammar; L(G) is the resulting language. The condition w ∈ Σ* excludes unfinished strings containing variables. Thus S ⇒* S is true, but S itself is not a terminal word of L(G). ε belongs only if S can derive ε.

sections.title: Keep the whole current string visible
sections.html:
S → aSb | ε
S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaaSbbb ⇒ aaabbb

Each arrow changes one occurrence. The last step uses S → ε. It does not erase any existing a or b.

Write the current sentential form after every replacement. Beside it, record the rule used when the derivation is long. Do not jump from one line to another by silently applying several rules.

sections.title: Leftmost and rightmost are replacement orders
sections.html:
A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining variable. A rightmost derivation always expands the rightmost remaining variable. “Leftmost” does not mean replace the first character; it means find the first variable when reading from the left.

E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → number | ( E )

In E + T, a leftmost derivation expands E next; a rightmost derivation expands T next. Both can produce the same parse tree. Different expansion orders alone do not make a grammar ambiguous.

sections.title: Read target structure before choosing a rule
sections.html:
For an expression, identify the outermost operation, excluding operators inside parentheses. For (2 + 5) * 8, multiplication is outside the parentheses, so begin with a structure that has multiplication at its root.

For a list or program, identify its fixed punctuation first, then expand the parts inside it. A terminal already placed in the wrong position cannot later be rewritten away. A premature wrong terminal is a reason to revise the preceding production choice.

worked.title: Leftmost and rightmost derivations of 2 + 3 * 4
worked.intro:
Use this supplied grammar, with start variable E:

E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → number | ( E )
Target: 2 + 3 * 4

The expression is grouped as 2 + (3 * 4). E combines terms using +; T combines factors using *; F supplies a number or a parenthesized expression. The rule F → number is shown with each token’s actual text below. We will finish the same production structure in two different orders.

steps.title: Identify the outer structure
steps.html: The top-level addition splits the expression into 2 and 3 * 4. Start E ⇒ E + T.

steps.title: Complete the leftmost subexpression
steps.html:
E ⇒ E + T
  ⇒ T + T
  ⇒ F + T
  ⇒ 2 + T

The T on the right remains untouched while the variables to its left are expanded.

steps.title: Finish the leftmost derivation
steps.html:
2 + T ⇒ 2 + T * F
      ⇒ 2 + F * F
      ⇒ 2 + 3 * F
      ⇒ 2 + 3 * 4

At each arrow, the selected variable is the leftmost one still present.

steps.title: Construct the rightmost derivation separately
steps.html:
E ⇒ E + T
  ⇒ E + T * F
  ⇒ E + T * 4
  ⇒ E + F * 4
  ⇒ E + 3 * 4
  ⇒ T + 3 * 4
  ⇒ F + 3 * 4
  ⇒ 2 + 3 * 4

The production structure is the same. Only the order in which its independent branches are completed changes.

practice.prompt: Give a complete derivation of 0011 using S → 0S1 | ε. Identify every sentential form.
practice.hint: Count how many applications of the recursive rule create two zeros.
practice.solution:
S ⇒ 0S1 ⇒ 00S11 ⇒ 0011

All four strings shown are sentential forms. The final one contains only terminals. There are two recursive applications and one terminating application.

practice.prompt: Using S → AB, A → aA | ε, B → bB | ε, give a leftmost derivation of aab.
practice.hint: Finish A before touching B.
practice.solution:
S ⇒ AB ⇒ aAB ⇒ aaAB ⇒ aaB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aab

The fourth arrow removes A with A → ε. The final arrow removes B. Expanding B before A disappears would break the leftmost requirement, though it could still be a valid unrestricted derivation.

check.prompt: In the sentential form aABb, which variable must a rightmost derivation expand next?
check.answer: B
check.explanation: B is the rightmost remaining variable. The terminal b to its right does not affect that choice.

transfer.prompt: Use E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → number | ( E ) to give both a leftmost and a rightmost derivation of (5 + 6) * 7. Keep every intermediate sentential form.

setup:
You can now apply a grammar rule. A derivation records those replacements in order, beginning at the start variable. Each whole intermediate string is a sentential form, which may still contain variables.

Notation or termMeaning in this lesson
α ⇒ βOne rule application changes the whole current string α into β. Alpha and beta are names for strings, not symbols to generate.
⇒*Zero or more applications. In particular, S ⇒* S uses no rule.
Leftmost / rightmostChoose the leftmost / rightmost remaining variable occurrence, ignoring terminals.
E, T, FVariables for an expression, a term, and a factor. Their exact permitted replacements are supplied in the example.

A number token can have actual text 2, 3 or 4. In the worked derivations we show that text directly: a step written F ⇒ 2 uses F → number for the token whose text is 2. You are not inventing a new F → 2 production. Parse-tree terminology is introduced next; this lesson only needs the sequence of replacements.
bridge: A derivation shows a sequence of replacements. Lesson 4 keeps those same choices in a tree, so you can see which variable generated each part.

title: Build parse trees for expressions and programs
summary: Start with a familiar derivation, learn what each part of a tree means, then build lists, expressions and small programs one rule at a time.
goals: Explain root, parent, child, leaf, subtree and yield using a small tree.
Turn each rule application into the exact ordered group of children.
Recognize a finished tree, including punctuation and ε productions.
Build a small program tree before attempting nested blocks and calls.

sections.title: The vocabulary, with a concrete meaning
sections.html:
You only need one drawing rule: when you use a production, make its right-hand-side symbols the chosen variable’s children, in that exact order. The following words describe parts of the resulting drawing.

WordMeaningIn the 0011 example
NodeOne labelled position in the tree.Each S, 0, 1 and ε label is a separate node.
RootThe starting node, with no parent.The top S.
Parent and childThe node being expanded and one symbol of its replacement.The root S is the parent of 0, the middle S and 1.
LeafA node with no children.The terminal 0 and 1 nodes, plus the displayed ε leaf.
SubtreeA node together with all the nodes underneath it.The middle S and everything generated from it form one subtree.
YieldThe terminal sequence from the leaves in grammar order; ε adds nothing.0011.

Two nodes can have the same label. The three S nodes are three different occurrences, with different parents. Choosing a rule at one occurrence does not expand any other S automatically.

We keep the children in order because the grammar generates a string. Swapping 0 and 1 would change the output. A completed tree has no unfinished variable leaf: every variable must have the children required by one of its productions.

sections.title: A procedure you can repeat for any supplied grammar
sections.html:
1. Copy the grammar, start variable and target. These are the starting information, not things you have to guess.
  2. Draw the start variable. This is the root of the whole tree.
  3. Choose one unfinished variable occurrence. Find a production whose output can fit that part of the target.
  4. Copy the right-hand side as its ordered children. Include every terminal, punctuation mark and variable. For an ε production, draw ε.
  5. Continue at the unfinished variables. Finish one subtree at a time if that makes the work easier.
  6. Check the productions and yield. Every parent-child group must match a supplied rule, and the terminal leaves must reproduce the whole target.

In these examples we build from the root toward the leaves. If a chosen rule puts a wrong terminal in the output, go back and revise that choice: terminals cannot be rewritten later.

Lesson 3’s leftmost and rightmost derivations tell you which variable to expand next. The tree records the chosen productions rather than the time you drew them. Finishing independent subtrees in a different order can give the same completed tree.

sections.title: Next: build the familiar one-item list
sections.html:
Use the list grammar from lesson 2, repeated here so you have every rule beside the example:

Start variable: S
S → [ L ]
L → ε | id T
T → ε | , id T
Target: [ id ]

id is one terminal token representing an item. S, L and T are variables. The brackets and comma are terminals. The letter T names the remaining list tail; it is not an extra input item.

Choose this ruleWhy it fits [ id ]Children to draw
S → [ L ]The whole list has brackets around its contents.[, L, ]
L → id TThe contents have one item, so they are not empty.id, T
T → εThere is no comma or additional item after the first id.ε
  • S
    • [
    • L
      • id
      • T
        • ε
    • ]

The yield is [ id ]. The T node stays in the tree because L → id T requires it; its ε child says that the rest is empty. Omitting T would leave the L node with the wrong children. For the empty list [ ], use L → ε instead. These are two different places where an empty component may occur.

sections.title: Then: read a small expression tree
sections.html:
This supplied expression grammar gives names to expressions and operators:

Start variable: E
E → E Op E | ( E ) | number
Op → + | *

E means an expression and Op means an operator. Both are variables. number, +, *, ( and ) are terminals. A label such as number: 2 is one number token showing the actual text 2; the colon is an annotation, not another input token.

Start with 2 + 5. The root E uses E → E Op E: an expression, an operator, and another expression. The first E uses E → number for 2. Op uses Op → +. The last E uses E → number for 5.

  • E
    • E
      • number: 2
    • Op
      • +
    • E
      • number: 5

The yield is number + number, with actual token text 2 + 5. Notice that Op must have its own + child. Putting + directly under the root would skip the Op required by the rule.

Add parentheses and multiplication: (2 + 5) * 8

The outermost operation is multiplication: the addition is inside parentheses. Use E → E Op E at the root, with the root Op producing *. Its first E uses E → ( E ), so the parentheses become two terminal children surrounding a new E. Build the 2 + 5 subtree under that new E, then finish the root’s last E as number 8.

  • E
    • E
      • (
      • E
        • E
          • number: 2
        • Op
          • +
        • E
          • number: 5
      • )
    • Op
      • *
    • E
      • number: 8

Terminal yield: ( number + number ) * number. Token text: (2 + 5) * 8. Every parenthesis belongs to the E that used E → ( E ). We will study ambiguity and precedence in lesson 7; for now, follow the explicit grouping in this target.

sections.title: Read the program grammar before using it
sections.html:
The next examples use a small supplied programming language. You do not need to know a particular programming language or invent its rules. We are only showing how its tokens are grouped. Spaces and indentation separate tokens for readability; they are not terminal leaves here.

Start variable: Function
Function → def id ( Params ) Block
Params → ε | id ParamTail
ParamTail → ε | , id ParamTail
Block → { Stmts }
Stmts → ε | Stmt Stmts
Stmt → If | Return
If → if ( Expr ) Block
Return → return Expr
Expr → id | id . Expr | id ( Args )
Args → ε | Expr ArgTail
ArgTail → ε | , Expr ArgTail

A name appearing on the left of an arrow is a variable. A multi-letter name such as ParamTail labels one variable node. Keywords such as return and punctuation such as { are terminals. Case matters in these rules: Return is a variable, while lowercase return is a terminal keyword.

VariableWhat this part represents
FunctionThe complete function definition; this grammar’s start variable.
Params / ParamTailThe parameter names inside the function header’s parentheses / the remaining comma-and-name groups.
BlockAn opening brace, its statement list, and a closing brace.
Stmts / StmtA list of zero or more statements / exactly one statement.
If / ReturnOne if statement / one return statement.
ExprA name, a member access such as cursor.link, or a function call.
Args / ArgTailThe expressions supplied in a call / the remaining comma-and-expression groups.

id is a terminal category for a name. A leaf labelled id: cursor means one id token whose text is cursor. It does not mean cursor is a new variable or needs its own production.

Read Function → def id ( Params ) Block aloud as: “A Function produces the keyword def, a name, an opening parenthesis, the parameters, a closing parenthesis, and a block.” It has six children. Params and Block need further expansion; the other four children are already terminal leaves.

sections.html:

sections.title: Understand the list tails before adding more items
sections.html:
The list rules all use the same idea: produce one item, then leave a variable for the rest. The rest either adds another item or becomes ε.

Two parameters: x,y

Params ⇒ id ParamTail
       ⇒ id , id ParamTail
       ⇒ id , id

The first id has text x; the second has text y. ParamTail → , id ParamTail contributes a comma and one more name together. The last ParamTail uses ε.

  • Params
    • id: x
    • ParamTail
      • ,
      • id: y
      • ParamTail
        • ε

Two arguments: probe(cursor.link,y)

Parameters are names declared in the function header. Arguments are expressions supplied in a call. That is why Params uses id, while Args uses Expr. For this call, choose Expr → id ( Args ) for probe. The first argument is cursor.link, built with Expr → id . Expr and then Expr → id. The second is y, built with Expr → id.

Args ⇒ Expr ArgTail
     ⇒ Expr , Expr ArgTail
     ⇒ Expr , Expr

This last sequence expands only the argument-list structure; each Expr still needs its own expansion. The comma belongs to ArgTail. Here is the complete call tree, with both expressions finished:

  • Expr
    • id: probe
    • (
    • Args
      • Expr
        • id: cursor
        • .
        • Expr
          • id: link
      • ArgTail
        • ,
        • Expr
          • id: y
        • ArgTail
          • ε

Several statements inside one block

Stmts represents a whole list, while Stmt represents one statement. To make a list with two statements, expand its list structure like this:

sections.title: Check a tree before moving to practice
sections.html:
CheckWhat to look for
StartThe root is the specified start variable. A requested subtree starts at its specified variable.
Each productionA variable’s immediate children, in order, are exactly one supplied right-hand side.
CompletionEvery variable has been expanded. A leftover Expr or Stmts leaf is unfinished.
Punctuation and empty rulesParentheses, braces, dots and commas remain as terminals; each chosen ε production is visible.
YieldReading terminal leaves in order, with ε omitted, reproduces every target token and no extra ones.

For example, attaching return directly under Stmts skips Stmt and Return, so it fails the production check even if the visible words look right. Leaving out a comma fails the yield check. A shortened diagram that keeps only operations is often called an abstract syntax tree; this lesson asks for the complete grammar-based parse tree.

Begin the practice with one small tree. Keep the rules visible while you work. The larger nested example is there to show how repeated small steps fit together.

worked.title: From a familiar derivation to your first complete tree
worked.intro:
In lesson 3, a derivation showed the whole current string after each replacement. A parse tree keeps the same rule choices and shows which variable produced each group of symbols. We will build a tree using rules you have already used:

Start variable: S
S → 0S1 | ε
Target string: 0011
Known derivation: S ⇒ 0S1 ⇒ 00S11 ⇒ 0011

Here is the complete result first. Each label is a node. The top S is the root. A line going down from one node reaches one of its children; the upper node is their parent. Nodes with no children are leaves.

Now follow how each rule creates part of this tree. You do not need to invent any grammar rules or know how to parse a program yet.

Begin with one node labelled S, because S is this grammar’s start variable. It is unfinished: S is a variable, so it still needs a rule. A variable does not become a terminal just because we have not drawn its children yet.

A derivation replaces a variable in the current string. A tree keeps that variable as a parent and draws the replacement underneath it. Both describe the same production choices. Your task is to show every choice and check the final leaves.
