steps.title: Test the closest invalid strings
steps.html: pqqrrss has two ss but only one p, so the second s cannot pop A. ppqrrs has two rs but only one q, so the second r cannot pop B. ppqqss has no r, and the required first-r state cannot be reached.

practice.prompt: Why should the inner and outer markers be different?
practice.hint: The inner phase must know when to stop.
practice.solution: Different markers let the r phase remove only B and let the inner cleanup stop at A. If both dependencies used A, a missing q could be hidden by consuming an outer p marker, admitting an invalid string.

practice.prompt: Give a grammar for aⁱbʲcʲdⁱ with i,j ≥ 1.
practice.hint: Force a positive base in both nested components.
practice.solution:
S → a S d | a T d
T → b T c | b c

S always creates at least one a/d pair. T always creates at least one b/c pair. No independent extra-opening-symbol component is present, so both matches are equalities.

practice.prompt: Can the B-discard phase read an r after it has removed all Bs?
practice.hint: State what an r requires.
practice.solution: No. Every r requires a distinct previous q represented by B. Once the phase has declared the r block finished, it should have no r-reading transitions. This prevents leftover input from changing which qs were counted as extras.

check.prompt: For stack BBAAAZ, which dependency must be completed first?
check.answer: The dependency represented by B.
check.explanation: A stack accesses only its top, and the Bs represent the inner q/r dependency.

transfer.prompt: For the same p/q/r/s block order, adapt the grammar to {pⁱqʲrᵏsⁱ : i ≥ 1 and 1 ≤ k ≤ j}. The outer counts must now be equal; the inner closing count stays positive and surplus qs are still allowed. Explain exactly which rule component you remove and why.
transfer.solution:
S → p S s | p T s
T → q T r | q Q r
Q → q Q | ε

Removing P removes the source of extra ps. Each p is now paired with exactly one s. The inner grammar still allows surplus qs and forces at least one q/r pair. A corresponding PDA must reject if any A remains after the last s; it may still discard surplus Bs after the r block.

setup:
Lesson 11 introduced nested matches, and lesson 12 allowed a surplus. Here both ideas occur in one four-block language:

{pⁱqʲrᵏsˡ : 1 ≤ l ≤ i and 1 ≤ k ≤ j}

Read it as: at least one s and no more ss than ps; at least one r and no more rs than qs. All ps come first, then qs, then rs, then ss. Thus every block is nonempty.

The q/r match is inside the p/s match. Use B markers for qs above A markers for ps, so the inner Bs are removed first. Surplus opening symbols may be discarded only after the corresponding closing block has actually begun. An ε discard consumes no input and cannot stand in for a required first r or s.
bridge: Block order let us use separate push, match and cleanup phases. Lesson 14 changes the problem: equal counts are required even when the input symbols alternate.

title: Count symbols in arbitrary order
summary: Use cancellation rather than ordered push-then-pop phases when symbols can alternate.
goals: Distinguish arbitrary-order equality from equal consecutive blocks.
Maintain a signed difference using two stack symbols.
Construct a grammar and PDA that allow neutral symbols anywhere.

sections.title: Order changes the required method
sections.html:
{aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} requires all as before all bs. In contrast, {w ∈ {a,b}* : |w|a = |w|b} includes ab, ba, abab, and bbaa. Read |w|a as “the number of occurrences of a in w.” It is a count, not the length of a block.

A one-way push-as-then-pop-bs machine rejects valid arbitrary-order strings such as ba. Instead maintain the difference balance = number of as read − number of bs read.

sections.title: Choose a signed stack invariant
sections.html:
When the balance is positive, its magnitude is the number of As above Z. When it is negative, its magnitude is the number of Bs above Z. At balance zero the stack is Z. As and Bs never occur together above Z.

ReadTopReplacementEffect
aZAZStart positive surplus
aAAAIncrease positive surplus
aBεCancel one b
bZBZStart negative surplus
bBBBIncrease negative surplus
bAεCancel one a

Each row consumes exactly one input symbol. At the end, equality holds exactly when Z is visible.

sections.title: Allow neutral symbols
sections.html:
For {w ∈ {a,b,c,d}* : |w|a = |w|b}, c and d are neutral. Read either symbol while leaving the stack unchanged: c,T/T and d,T/T for every T in {A,B,Z}.

Neutral characters may appear before, between, and after the counted characters. A construction that allows c/d only in one fixed block is too restrictive.

sections.title: A grammar for arbitrary-order equality
sections.html:
E → a E b E | b E a E | c E | d E | ε

The first two alternatives add one a and one b, in either order, and permit balanced substrings between and after them. The cE and dE rules add a neutral symbol. Every production preserves equal a/b counts.

Why can it generate every equal-count string? If the first symbol is neutral, remove it and recurse. If it is a, choose the first later position where the running a-minus-b difference returns to zero; that position is b. The inside and the remaining suffix each have equal counts, giving a E b E. The argument with b is symmetric.

That explanation checks completeness, rather than only observing that the grammar has balanced production counts.

worked.title: Trace b a a c b d
worked.intro:
Target input: baacbd. Start in q with stack Z, top on the left. The full update rules are:

ReadTopReplacement
aZAZ
aAAA
aBε
bZBZ
bBBB
bAε
c or dT ∈ {A,B,Z}T

Each row consumes its input symbol and stays in q. Finish by ε,Z/ε to done, which has no outgoing transitions. This is empty-stack NPDA acceptance after full input consumption. The numeric balance changes on a/b only; the input character d is neutral.

steps.title: Read b
steps.html:
(q, baacbd, Z) → (q, aacbd, BZ)

There is one more b than a so far: balance = −1.

steps.title: Read a and cancel
steps.html:
(q, aacbd, BZ) → (q, acbd, Z)

The counts are equal again. The stack returns to Z.

steps.title: Read the next a
steps.html:
(q, acbd, Z) → (q, cbd, AZ)

Now balance = 1. The stack changes sign by first passing through Z.

steps.title: Ignore c for counting
steps.html:
(q, cbd, AZ) → (q, bd, AZ)

The c transition consumes c but keeps A. Neutral does not mean unread.

steps.title: Read b, then d, then finish
steps.html:
(q, bd, AZ) → (q, d, Z)
→ (q, ε, Z) → (done, ε, ε)

The b cancels A. The d is consumed without changing Z. Equality and full input consumption both hold.

practice.prompt: Trace abba using the signed-stack method.
practice.hint: After the third symbol the surplus changes sign.
practice.solution:
Z → AZ → Z → BZ → Z

The stack contents after a, b, b, a encode differences +1, 0, −1, 0. The string is accepted after the finishing condition.

practice.prompt: Why is S → a S b | b S a | ε incomplete for arbitrary-order equal counts?
practice.hint: Try the string abba.
practice.solution: Any nonempty generated string has opposite first and last symbols. abba starts and ends with a, so this grammar cannot generate it even though its counts are equal. The grammar needs concatenation capacity, such as the second E in a E b E and b E a E.

practice.prompt: Give a derivation of abba using E → a E b E | b E a E | ε.
practice.hint: Split after the first ab.
practice.solution:
E ⇒ a E b E ⇒ a b E
⇒ a b b E a E ⇒ a b b a E ⇒ a b b a

The first pair forms ab. The final E generates ba, showing why a balanced suffix component is needed.

check.prompt: Does the stack need to preserve the full order of previously read a and b symbols to test equal counts?
check.answer: No.
check.explanation: The signed difference is sufficient. The stack records the surplus count and its sign.

transfer.prompt: Construct the signed-stack rules for |w|c = |w|d over {a,b,c,d}. State what a and b do.
transfer.solution:
Use C for surplus c and D for surplus d. On c: Z → CZ, C → CC, D → ε. On d: Z → DZ, D → DD, C → ε. Consume a or b while preserving the current top symbol. At the end, accept exactly when only Z remains. The corresponding grammar is F → c F d F | d F c F | a F | b F | ε.

To make the acceptance rule explicit, start in q with Z and use those updates as q loops. Add ε,Z/ε from q to a halt state done with no outgoing transitions. This is an NPDA with empty-stack acceptance after all input is consumed. The early cleanup branch fails if any input remains.

setup:
Earlier count machines required blocks such as aⁿbⁿ. This language permits a and b in any order. For example, ba and abba must both be accepted. A phase that permanently switches from reading a to reading b cannot handle that.

Maintain a balance: the number of as read minus the number of bs read. Positive balance is stored as As; negative balance is stored as Bs; zero balance leaves only Z. Reading an opposite symbol cancels one stored surplus. The stack never needs As and Bs together.

c and d are neutral here: they are still consumed, but do not change the balance. The input symbol d and the numeric balance are different things. In the transition rules, T stands for any currently allowed top symbol, not a new fixed stack marker.
bridge: The signed surplus is enough to test one arbitrary-order equality. Lesson 15 combines alternative tests and uses nondeterminism when a phase boundary is hidden.

title: Use nondeterminism for alternatives and hidden boundaries
summary: Keep each branch complete, and accept only when one whole branch succeeds.
goals: Translate an OR condition into grammar and PDA branches.
Distinguish a hidden midpoint from a visible separator.
Explain acceptance and rejection using complete runs.

sections.title: Union means one successful alternative
sections.html:
If L = L₁ ∪ L₂, a string belongs when it is in at least one component. The components may overlap; a string satisfying both is still accepted. A grammar uses S → S₁ | S₂, with separate nonterminal names for the component grammars.

An NPDA uses a fresh start state with ε branches into the two component machines. Each component must finish its own complete test. Rejecting in one branch does not reject the whole NPDA if another branch accepts.

sections.title: An OR of two count equalities
sections.html:
Consider strings over {a,b,c,d} satisfying “a-count equals b-count OR c-count equals d-count.” Build one signed-counter component for the first equality, treating c/d as neutral, and another for the second, treating a/b as neutral.

S → E | F
E → a E b E | b E a E | c E | d E | ε
F → c F d F | d F c F | a F | b F | ε

The two grammars are alternatives. Do not run the first test, reset its counter, and call that proof of the second test: both properties refer to the same complete input string.

sections.title: A midpoint that must be guessed
sections.html:
For even palindromes {w wᴿ : w ∈ {0,1}*}, the input contains no separator telling the machine when the first half ends. Here wᴿ means w written in reverse order. A PDA can nondeterministically switch from storing symbols to matching symbols.

In the store state, read 0 and push A or read 1 and push B. On a guessed ε switch, enter match. In match, read 0 only when the top is A, and read 1 only when the top is B, removing that marker. Finish only when the bottom marker is reached with the whole input consumed.

For odd palindromes, another transition may consume exactly one middle symbol without pushing or popping. Do not silently add this option when the target language includes only even palindromes.

sections.title: Why a failed guess is harmless
sections.html:
An NPDA does not require every branch to accept. An early midpoint guess leaves unmatched input; a late guess leaves unmatched stack symbols. Neither branch accepts. The correct midpoint branch accepts exactly when the second half reverses the first.

With a visible separator, as in {w # wᴿ}, switch on # instead of guessing. This removes that source of nondeterminism. Formal determinism and acceptance-convention limits are examined in the equivalence lessons.

worked.title: Recognize 0110 by guessing a midpoint
worked.intro:
Target input: 0110. Start in store with stack Z, top on the left. A records a stored 0 and B a stored 1. Here T is a placeholder for each of the listed top symbols:

StateReadRequired topReplacementNext state
store0T ∈ {A,B,Z}ATstore
store1T ∈ {A,B,Z}BTstore
storeεT ∈ {A,B,Z}Tmatch
match0Aεmatch
match1Bεmatch
matchεZεdone

done has no outgoing transitions. Accept by empty stack only after all input is consumed. The ε move from store to match guesses the midpoint without reading or altering input. We follow the branch that guesses after two symbols.

steps.title: Store the first symbol
steps.html:
(store, 0110, Z) → (store, 110, AZ)

The first 0 creates an A obligation.

steps.title: Store the next symbol
steps.html:
(store, 110, AZ) → (store, 10, BAZ)

The most recently stored symbol is now on top.

steps.title: Choose the midpoint
steps.html:
(store, 10, BAZ) → (match, 10, BAZ)

The ε move consumes nothing and preserves the entire stack.

steps.title: Match in reverse order
steps.html:
(match, 10, BAZ) → (match, 0, AZ)
→ (match, ε, Z)

The first symbol of the second half is 1, which matches top B. The next is 0, which matches A.

steps.title: Finish and compare a wrong guess
steps.html: Remove Z into the empty-stack halt state. A branch that switched after just the initial 0 would next see 1 with A on top, so it rejects. That failed branch does not invalidate the successful midpoint branch.

practice.prompt: For the OR-of-equalities language, does aabc belong? Which branch succeeds?
practice.hint: Count a/b separately from c/d.
practice.solution: a-count = 2 and b-count = 1, so the first equality fails. c-count = 1 and d-count = 0, so the second fails too. The string is rejected. An OR requires at least one true equality, not merely the presence of a matching pair somewhere.

practice.prompt: Does aab belong to that language?
practice.hint: The second equality can hold with both counts zero.
practice.solution: Yes. a-count ≠ b-count, but c-count = d-count = 0. The F branch accepts. A construction that requires c and d to occur would wrongly reject this valid case.

practice.prompt: Why is 010 excluded by the even-palindrome PDA even though it is a palindrome?
practice.hint: Write its length as 2n or 2n + 1.
practice.solution: The language w wᴿ has even length. The machine’s midpoint switch consumes zero symbols, so every input symbol must be paired with another. Accepting odd palindromes requires a separately specified center-symbol transition.

check.prompt: For an NPDA, must every branch accept the input?
check.answer: No.
check.explanation: One finite accepting branch is sufficient. The input is rejected when no finite branch reaches an accepting configuration; an infinite branch does not cancel an accepting one.

transfer.prompt: Design a PDA plan for {w # wᴿ : w ∈ {a,b}*}. Give one accepted and two rejected tests.
transfer.solution: Before #, push A for a and B for b. Consume exactly one # and enter match. After #, read a only while removing A and b only while removing B. Do not permit further # symbols. Finish only with no unmatched markers and no unread input. ab#ba is accepted. ab#ab is rejected for the wrong reverse order; ab#b is rejected because A remains. # is also accepted, representing w = ε.

setup:
Lesson 14 checked one count equality. Union, written ∪, combines alternatives: a string is allowed if at least one complete condition holds. Both conditions refer to the same whole input, not to two separate substrings. Equal zero counts also satisfy an equality.

A nondeterministic branch is one possible sequence of configurations. Branches keep their own state, unread input and stack. An NPDA accepts if some finite branch consumes all input and meets the acceptance rule; it is not choosing randomly.

The worked example uses a different reason for branching: an even palindrome has no visible middle marker. Store a prefix, take an ε move to guess its end, then match the rest in reverse. A for 0 and B for 1 record symbol values, rather than just counts.
bridge: One successful branch proves NPDA acceptance. Lesson 16 removes guessing for selected languages by making every next action, including the end-of-input action, explicit.

title: Build deterministic runs and test a complete PDA
summary: Construct bracket and ratio machines, state the end-of-input convention, and test boundaries.
goals: Write deterministic transitions for visible nesting and weighted counts.
State precisely how the end of input is detected.
Turn a transition table into a reproducible simulator test plan.

sections.title: State the convention before drawing
sections.html:
A deterministic PDA has at most one enabled move in each situation. In the standard definition, an ε move with a given state and stack top cannot compete with an input-consuming move for that same state and top.

For the constructions below, $ is an explicit right-end marker appended after the original input. It is a new symbol that does not occur in the language’s original alphabet. The empty-stack machine processes w$; it removes Z only when it reads $. Do not silently describe this as an unmarked-input empty-stack DPDA. The equivalent unmarked recognizer can use final-state acceptance.

Optional: why unmarked deterministic empty-stack acceptance needs care

Without an end marker, ordinary empty-stack DPDAs accept only prefix-free languages under the standard stack-access definition. Balanced parentheses include ε and have accepted strings that are proper prefixes of other accepted strings, so that convention needs attention. See the determinism lesson for the proof and the distinction between an explicit marker and an external “input finished” simulator rule.

sections.title: Balanced parentheses: record unmatched opens
sections.html:
The depth is opens read minus closes read. Reading ( increases depth; reading ) decreases it and must never make it negative. Accept when depth is zero at the end. Balanced strings may concatenate: ()() is valid even though the stack returns to the bottom between its two pairs.

Use A for one unmatched (. With top T in {A,Z}: read ( and replace T by AT. Read ) with A on top and remove A. There is no ) transition on Z, so an unmatched close rejects. Read $ on Z and remove Z into halt. There is no $ transition on A, so unmatched opens reject. No ε transition competes with these moves.

sections.title: A final-state version with no end marker
sections.html:
Use state zero as accepting and state positive as nonaccepting. Start in zero with Z. Reading ( from zero pushes A and enters positive. In positive, reading ( pushes A. Reading ) pops A and enters a separate inspect state. inspect has only ε moves: if the new top is A, preserve A and return to positive; if it is Z, preserve Z and enter zero.

Because inspect has no input-consuming transitions, these forced ε moves are deterministic. zero has no ) transition. At the end of the unmarked input, acceptance is exactly being in zero. Repeated balanced components and ε are accepted while Z remains.

sections.title: A ratio machine: one x requires two ys
sections.html:
For {xⁿy²ⁿ : n ≥ 0}, use states xphase, yphase, and halt. Start with Z. Reading x in xphase replaces Z by AAZ or A by AAA: a net addition of two As. The first y requires A, removes it, and enters yphase. Every later y in yphase removes one A. No x transition exists in yphase.

In xphase or yphase, reading $ with Z on top removes Z and enters halt. This accepts ε via input $ and positive cases only after all obligations have been matched. A simulator limited to single pushes can expand a two-A push into a consumed-x transition followed by a forced ε transition through a fresh state.

sections.title: Enter, trace, test, and export
sections.html:
1. Write the alphabet, stack alphabet, initial marker, acceptance mode, and transition table before using a simulator.
  2. Create the states and mark the initial state. Use the simulator’s documented empty-stack or final-state setting; a drawn double circle does not by itself select empty-stack acceptance.
  3. Enter each transition’s input, pop, and push fields. Interface labels differ, so confirm which field is which using a one-step trace.
  4. Confirm push-string order by pushing two distinct symbols in a temporary test: identify which one is popped first. Translate from our top-left convention if needed.
  5. Test accepted strings, rejected near-misses, ε, and phase-boundary cases. If using $, append it to every test exactly once.
  6. Step through one accepted and one rejected input, recording state, unread input, and stack after each move.
  7. Save the simulator’s editable text/source representation and an image of the diagram if those export options are available. Reopen the editable file and repeat a short test.

These are model-based steps rather than claims about specific button names. Check the current automatonsimulator interface for its exact controls and whether it supplies an external end-of-input rule. State that rule alongside your diagram.

worked.title: Test the deterministic ratio machine on xxyyyy$
worked.intro:
Recognize the marked input xxyyyy$. Start in xphase with stack Z, top on the left. The complete DPDA table is:

StateReadRequired topReplacementNext state
xphasexZAAZxphase
xphasexAAAAxphase
xphaseyAεyphase
yphaseyAεyphase

yphase$Zεhalt

halt has no outgoing transitions; any missing transition rejects. Each x adds two future y matches. Read $ exactly once at the true end of the input. A successful run consumes it and empties the stack. No ε move is needed in this table.

steps.title: Initialize and read the first x
steps.html:
(xphase, xxyyyy$, Z)
→ (xphase, xyyyy$, AAZ)

Two As represent the two ys owed by the first x.

steps.title: Read the second x
steps.html:
(xphase, xyyyy$, AAZ)
→ (xphase, yyyy$, AAAAZ)

Replace top A by AAA, adding two As rather than three.

steps.title: Switch to the y phase
steps.html:
(xphase, yyyy$, AAAAZ)
→ (yphase, yyy$, AAAZ)

The first y removes one A. After this move, x is permanently forbidden.

steps.title: Match the remaining ys
steps.html:
(yphase, yyy$, AAAZ)
→ (yphase, yy$, AAZ)
→ (yphase, y$, AZ)
→ (yphase, $, Z)

There are exactly four y symbols for two x symbols.

steps.title: Consume the marker and finish
steps.html:
(yphase, $, Z) → (halt, ε, ε)

For xxyyy$, A remains and $ has no transition. For xxyyyyy$, an extra y is encountered with Z on top and has no transition. For xyxyy$, the later x is forbidden in yphase.

practice.prompt: Trace ()()$ in the end-marked bracket machine. Why does the first return to Z not accept early?
practice.hint: The only Z-removing move reads $.
practice.solution:
Z → AZ → Z → AZ → Z → ε

The moves read (, ), (, ), $. At the intermediate Z, the next input is (, so the machine pushes A again. It removes Z only on the actual right-end marker.

practice.prompt: Give three rejected bracket tests that check different errors.
practice.hint: Test negative depth, positive final depth, and an invalid prefix.
practice.solution: )$ rejects because ) cannot read on Z. (()$ rejects because A remains at $. ())($ rejects at its third symbol, before its total counts later return to equality. Equal total counts alone are not sufficient for balanced order.

practice.prompt: What is the net number of As added by replacing A with AAA?
practice.hint: Count the old top symbol as removed.
practice.solution: Two. The old A is removed and three As are inserted. The total goes from k to k + 2. A replacement A → AA adds only one and would implement the wrong ratio.

check.prompt: In the marked empty-stack constructions, when may Z be removed?
check.answer: Only when reading the explicit right-end marker $.
check.explanation: That prevents a finishing ε move from competing with ordinary input moves on Z.

transfer.prompt: Construct an end-marked empty-stack DPDA for {aⁿb³ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Include its invariant and boundary tests.
transfer.solution: In the a phase, each a pushes three As: Z → AAAZ and A → AAAA. The first b removes A and enters the b phase; later bs remove A. No a is allowed in the b phase. In either phase, read $ on Z to remove Z and halt. After reading aⁿbʲ in the b phase, the stack is A³ⁿ⁻ʲZ. Accept $, abbb$, and aabbbbbb$. Reject abb$ (only two bs), abbbb$ (one extra b), and abbabbbb$ (invalid order). Describe the accepted original language as strings w whose marked form w$ is accepted.

setup:
Previous NPDAs could guess when to switch or finish. A deterministic PDA (DPDA) has at most one enabled next move for a state and stack top. An enabled ε move cannot compete with an input-reading move for that same state and top.

This lesson makes the end visible by appending $. The original ratio language is {xⁿy²ⁿ : n ≥ 0}; the machine reads its marked form w$. Thus the empty original string is tested as $. The bottom marker Z is removed only while reading that final marker.

Each x owes two later ys. Replacing Z by AAZ adds two As; replacing A by AAA also adds two, because the old top A is removed first. The states enforce x-before-y order, while the stack enforces the ratio. Keep these two jobs separate.
bridge: A deterministic construction depends on its declared acceptance and input conventions. Lesson 17 introduces a general grammar conversion that may be nondeterministic even when another recognizer for the language is deterministic.

title: Turn a grammar into a PDA
summary: Use the stack to store the part of a leftmost derivation that still needs to match the input.
goals: Explain what the CFG–PDA equivalence theorem says and what it does not say.
Translate every grammar production and every terminal into a PDA transition.
Put a production onto the stack in the correct order and state an exact acceptance condition.

sections.title: Read the grammar-generated stack correctly
sections.html:
The example’s stack alphabet contains S, x, y and #. A top S means “choose a production”; a top x or y means “match this terminal next”; # means that no grammar symbols remain above the marker.

The grammar S → xSy | ε adds one x and one y per recursion and then removes S. The machine recreates those choices while checking an already supplied input. Choosing a production and reading a terminal therefore require separate moves.

sections.title: The equivalence theorem, read carefully
sections.html:
For any language L, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. L is context-free.
  2. Some context-free grammar G generates exactly L.
  3. Some nondeterministic pushdown automaton M recognizes exactly L.

“Equivalent” means that the descriptions determine the same set of accepted or generated strings. It does not mean the grammar and machine have the same number of rules, or that their steps look identical. The theorem gives a conversion in both directions. It does not promise a deterministic PDA for every CFG.

S ⇒* w means “there is a derivation from S to w using zero or more productions.” L(G) = {w ∈ Σ* : S ⇒* w} collects the terminal strings obtained this way. The machine construction must accept all these strings and reject every other string.

sections.title: What the stack represents
sections.html:
A sentential form contains terminals and variables, such as xxSyy. During a leftmost derivation the PDA stores the unmatched part of this form. If the matched input prefix is xx and the stack is Syy#, then concatenating the prefix with the stack above # gives xxSyy.

The invariant is:

matched input prefix + grammar symbols above #
= a sentential form in a leftmost derivation

The marker # is not part of the sentential form. When a variable is on top, choose a production for that variable. When a terminal is on top, match it against the next input symbol and pop it. Thus the top is the next grammar symbol to process; it is not always a nonterminal. After the preceding terminals are matched, the variable exposed on top is the leftmost unresolved variable.

sections.title: The general recipe
sections.html:
Let G = (V, Σ, P, S). Here V contains variables, Σ contains terminals, P contains productions, and S is the start variable.

  1. Create start, work, and halt states. The initial stack contains the protected marker #. Add start → work: ε, #/S# to push S above it once.
  2. Use stack alphabet Γ = V ∪ Σ ∪ {#}, where # is a fresh symbol.
  3. For every production A → α, add a work-state loop ε, A/α.
  4. For every terminal a ∈ Σ, add a work-state loop a, a/ε.
  5. Add work → halt: ε, #/ε and give halt no outgoing transitions. Accept only after full input consumption and empty stack. The initial marker prevents a zero-step empty-stack acceptance.

In input, pop/push notation, ε in the input position means “consume no input.” ε in the push position means “push nothing.” For a production A → ε, you still pop A; you do not pop or match a literal ε character.

Several productions with the same left-hand variable create several enabled choices. This is allowed in a PDA. A branch that chooses badly may fail; acceptance needs one successful complete branch.

sections.title: Push strings in the order that gives the right top
sections.html:
Our abstract replacement A → XYZ requires X on top, followed by Y, then Z. If a simulator supports a whole replacement string with leftmost-on-top semantics, enter XYZ. If it supports only individual pushes, pop A, then push Z, Y, X using private intermediate states.

old stack: Aβ
push Z:    Zβ
push Y:    YZβ
push X:    XYZβ

The intermediate states must belong only to this expansion. Do not let input matching or an unrelated production interrupt it. For A → ε, the expansion is simply a pop.

Check the simulator convention with a two-symbol example before entering a full grammar. Replace A by xy and inspect whether x is next to pop. The required result is fixed even when interfaces use different entry conventions.

sections.title: If you prefer final-state acceptance
sections.html:
Keep the same initial stack #, initialisation ε,#/S#, production loops, terminal-matching loops, and cleanup ε,#/ε. Mark halt as a final state and still require full input consumption. Then this particular construction finishes with both a final state and empty stack.

A nullable grammar (one whose start variable can derive ε) can reach halt without reading input, but it must still initialise, derive ε, and remove the marker. A nonnullable grammar cannot empty its stack immediately: # remains until all generated grammar symbols have been processed. If cleanup occurs while unread input remains, halt has no outgoing moves, so that branch fails.

worked.title: Build the recognizer for S → xSy | ε
worked.intro:
Start with this grammar:

S → xSy | ε

It generates ε, xy, xxyy, xxxyyy, …. A grammar creates one of these strings by rewriting S. The equivalent PDA receives a string and tries to recreate a derivation while checking the input.

JobTransition
Replace the preloaded bottom marker with S above that markerstart → work: ε, #/S#
Choose the recursive productionwork → work: ε, S/xSy
Choose the empty productionwork → work: ε, S/ε
Match an xwork → work: x, x/ε
Match a ywork → work: y, y/ε
Finish after removing every grammar symbolwork → halt: ε, #/ε

The initial stack is #, and the halt state has no outgoing transitions. This version accepts by empty stack after all input is consumed. The marker prevents acceptance before initialisation. Its stack is written with the top at the left. The transition ε, S/xSy therefore replaces top S with xSy above the untouched marker, leaving x on top.

Input to trace: xxyy. We now follow one successful branch using exactly the table just given. The initial state is start; the processing state is work.

steps.title: Initialise the representation
steps.html: Begin with stack # and take ε,#/S#. The input is still xxyy; the stack is S#. Nothing has been consumed.

steps.title: Expand the first variable
steps.html: Take ε, S/xSy. The stack becomes xSy#. The production creates a terminal to check; it does not consume the first input x yet.

steps.title: Match and continue the leftmost derivation
steps.html: Take x, x/ε. The consumed prefix is x, the remaining input is xyy, and the stack is Sy#. Expand that S to xSy; the stack becomes xSyy#. Match the next x, leaving Syy#.

steps.title: End the recursive expansion
steps.html: Choose ε, S/ε. The stack becomes yy#. The consumed prefix is xx and the input still to check is yy. The represented sentential form is xxyy.

steps.title: Match the remaining terminals and test acceptance
steps.html: Use y, y/ε twice. The input is now ε and stack is #. Take ε,#/ε to halt; only then is the stack empty and this branch accepts. The corresponding grammar derivation is S ⇒ xSy ⇒ xxSyy ⇒ xxyy.

steps.title: Check a failed input as well
steps.html: For xxy, the branch above eventually consumes the only y and leaves one unmatched y on the stack. No terminal-match transition can finish. Other choices of recursion also fail, so the PDA rejects.

practice.prompt: Translate A → aA | b into production transitions, then list the terminal-matching transitions.
practice.hint: The input part is ε for a production; terminal matching consumes an actual terminal.
practice.solution: Use ε, A/aA and ε, A/b for the productions. Use a, a/ε and b, b/ε for matching. Start with # and use ε,#/A# for initialisation. Cleanup is ε,#/ε to a halt state with no outgoing transitions. These transitions recognize a*b. The production A → b puts b on the stack; a separate transition consumes b.

practice.prompt: A machine has stack Tz. It applies T → uv. Write the new stack and, for single-symbol pushes, the push order.
practice.hint: The stack suffix z remains below the entire replacement.
practice.solution: The new stack is uvz, top at the left. Pop T, push v, then push u. Pushing u and then v would instead leave vuz and try to match the wrong terminal first.

practice.prompt: For S → xSy | ε, can an empty stack alone certify acceptance of input xyxy?
practice.hint: Trace the branch that generates only the first xy.
practice.solution: No. That branch can remove its last grammar symbol after consuming the first xy and then pop # to halt, but input xy remains. Acceptance requires both input exhaustion and empty stack. In fact xyxy is not in {xⁿyⁿ}; the grammar has no concatenation production to create a second matched block.

check.prompt: When ε, A/aB is applied, is a consumed from the input?
check.answer: No. The machine pops A and replaces it with aB without consuming input.
check.explanation: The ε before the comma controls input consumption. A later a, a/ε transition must match the generated terminal.

transfer.prompt: Build an empty-stack PDA from S → aSb | c. State the stack convention, list every transition, and trace aacbb.
transfer.solution: Use top-left stacks and preload # and initialise with ε,#/S#. Add cleanup ε,#/ε to halt, with no outgoing transitions. Work loops: ε, S/aSb, ε, S/c, and a,a/ε, b,b/ε, c,c/ε. A successful stack trace is S# → aSb# → Sb# → aSbb# → Sbb# → cbb# → bb# → b# → # → ε. The matched terminals are a,a,c,b,b, in that order. The grammar derivation is S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aacbb. Accept only after the last b is consumed and the stack empties by removing #. It cannot accept ε at the initial configuration because # is present.

setup:
Lessons 9–16 designed stack meanings for particular languages. Now we use a general recipe that works for any supplied CFG. The stack holds grammar symbols still to process, including both variables and terminals.

There are two distinct actions: expand a top variable using a production without reading input, or match a top terminal by reading that same terminal and removing it. Putting x on the stack does not consume an input x.

We use # as a fresh stack bottom marker here. It plays the role Z played earlier and is not an input separator. Start with #, replace it by S#, and remove # only after the grammar symbols are gone. A successful branch must also have consumed all input. The complete transition table is supplied with the worked example.
bridge: Expansion and input matching are separate transitions. Lesson 18 writes both actions in one table and connects the stack to the current grammar derivation.

title: Trace a derivation and a PDA together
summary: Record every expansion and terminal match without mixing up the stack, input, and sentential form.
goals: Write a complete configuration trace for a grammar-derived PDA.
Keep consumed input, remaining input, and stack contents separate.
Explain why a terminal mismatch kills one branch and why one failed branch is not global rejection.

sections.title: Start with the whole problem
sections.html:
Use this grammar for balanced square brackets:

S → [S]S | ε

The first S inside brackets generates the nested part. The second S generates whatever comes after that complete pair. We will recognize [[]][]: one nested group followed by one simple pair.

The PDA has production loops ε,S/[S]S and ε,S/ε, terminal loops [,[/ε and ],]/ε, initial stack #, initialisation ε,#/S#, and cleanup ε,#/ε to a halt state with no outgoing transitions. It accepts by empty stack after the whole input has been consumed. Stack top is always written at the left.

sections.html:
Write a configuration as (state, remaining input, stack). For example, (work, ][], S]S#) says the next input symbol is ] but the next stack symbol to process is S. The PDA may still expand that S before matching anything.

Add a consumed-input column when explaining a run. Its contents must always be a prefix of the original input. The concatenation consumed + remaining stays equal to the original input at every step. Expansion changes the stack; matching changes the stack and input together.

Keep a separate sentential-form column if asked to connect the machine to a derivation. Terminal matching does not apply a production, so it does not change that form. It only moves the boundary between consumed prefix and the grammar symbols above #.

sections.title: Why this construction has the same language
sections.html:
L(G) ⊆ L(M) means that every string generated by the grammar is accepted by the machine. The reverse inclusion means every accepted string is generated. Proving both establishes equality.

Grammar to machine: take any leftmost derivation of a terminal string w. The PDA can choose those same productions. Whenever the derivation exposes terminals at the left, they match the next symbols of w. Eventually every grammar symbol is matched, and cleanup removes # to empty the stack.

Machine to grammar: take any accepting run. Read only the steps that replace variables. Those steps are grammar productions, in leftmost order. The matching steps certify that the resulting terminal string is exactly the input. Therefore an accepting run cannot invent a string outside the grammar.

These are two separate inclusion arguments: L(G) ⊆ L(M) and L(M) ⊆ L(G). Both are needed to establish equality.

sections.title: A wrong choice and an infinite choice are different
sections.html:
At step 3, input begins with [ and the stack is S]S#. If the branch chooses S → ε, the stack becomes ]S#. Now stack top ] disagrees with input [, so no terminal-matching transition applies. This branch fails. The successful branch instead expands S to [S]S.

With a left-recursive grammar such as E → EE | a, a branch can keep expanding the leftmost E forever. The existence of that infinite branch does not cancel a finite accepting branch. A practical simulator may use a step limit; “no accepting path found within the limit” is not a mathematical rejection proof.

setup:
Lesson 17 converted grammar rules to stack replacements. This lesson keeps four pieces of bookkeeping visible: the input already consumed, the input still unread, the stack, and the derivation represented by that stack.

Use S → [S]S | ε, with start variable S. The first S inside the brackets describes their contents; the last S describes a following balanced group. Top is on the left, and # is a stack bottom marker, not input. The machine starts in start with #, works in work, and finishes in halt.

On an expansion row, unread input stays fixed. On a match row, one input terminal and the matching stack terminal disappear together. At every row, consumed input followed by remaining input must still be the original target. We begin with the short input [] before reading the longer table.
bridge: The grammar-to-PDA argument proves the two descriptions have the same language. Lesson 19 builds the reverse conversion by giving grammar variables a precise meaning in a machine run.

title: Turn a PDA back into a grammar
summary: Represent a balanced part of a machine run with one variable for its entry and exit states.
goals: Explain why every PDA language has a CFG.
Read Xₚ,ᵩ as a variable describing a whole stack-balanced computation segment.
Apply the empty, concatenation, and matching-push/pop grammar rules to a small normalized PDA.

sections.title: Why the example splits at state s
sections.html:
The machine’s a-edge pushes A, and its b-edge pops A. At state s the stack is back at its starting height. The c/d pair then makes another balanced segment. This is why the grammar can concatenate a p-to-s variable with an s-to-f variable.

A useful variable here is one that can participate in a complete accepting derivation. The full construction produces many state-pair variables; the worked example lists only the rules needed for the unique abcd path.

sections.title: Prepare the machine before applying this recipe
sections.html:
Acceptance convention for this normal form: the run must reach its designated final state after consuming the whole input, and its stack must then be empty. An empty stack in a nonfinal state is not sufficient. This prevents an initially empty stack from accepting ε automatically.

This construction uses a normalized PDA with one accepting state, empty stack at the start and at acceptance, and transitions that push exactly one symbol or pop exactly one symbol. A transition does not both push and pop. It may read one input symbol or ε while performing that stack action.

  1. Introduce a fresh final state if there are several original final states.
  2. Introduce a fresh bottom marker and a cleanup phase so an accepting branch can empty its stack before reaching the new final state. Premature cleanup cannot accept because the whole input must still be consumed.
  3. Split a replace operation into a pop followed by single pushes, using fresh private states. Only the original step reads its input symbol; the added steps read ε.
  4. If a step changes no stack symbol, simulate it by pushing a fresh temporary symbol and immediately popping that symbol through a private state.

These transformations preserve the recognized language for a nondeterministic PDA. They need not preserve determinism. They are a preparation for proving the CFG–PDA theorem, not a promise that every final-state DPDA has an equivalent ordinary empty-stack DPDA.

sections.title: Give a state-pair variable a precise meaning
sections.html:
Create one variable Xₚ,ᵩ for every ordered pair of states p and q. Read it as “an input string that can take the machine from p to q while starting and ending with an empty stack.” More generally, the same segment can run above an untouched stack suffix: it never pops below its starting height.

This variable summarizes a whole computation segment, not a single edge. Its indices are states. They are not input symbols or stack symbols. There are at most |Q|² such variables, so the grammar remains finite.

If the normalized start state is q₀ and its unique final state is q𝒻, use Start → Xq₀,q𝒻. A string derived from this variable describes a complete accepting computation.

sections.title: Rule family 1: an empty segment
sections.html:
For every state p add:

Xₚ,ₚ → ε

Doing nothing consumes ε, leaves the stack untouched, and stays in the same state. Do not add Xₚ,ᵩ → ε for all unequal states p and q. A free jump between arbitrary states might recognize strings for which the machine has no run. An actual epsilon-input run between distinct states must be accounted for by its real stack operations and the other grammar rules.

sections.title: Rule family 2: concatenate balanced segments
sections.html:
For every triple p, r, q add:

Xₚ,ᵩ → Xₚ,ᵣ Xᵣ,ᵩ

The first segment takes p to r and restores the stack to its starting height. The second takes r to q and does the same. Their concatenation takes p to q. The shared state r is the exit state of the first segment and the entry state of the second.

This family handles runs that return to their starting stack height partway through. The two independently balanced groups ab and cd in the opening example are such a split.

sections.title: Rule family 3: match one push with its eventual pop
sections.html:
Suppose the machine has these transitions:

p -- read a, push T --> r
s -- read b, pop T  --> q

Add:

Xₚ,ᵩ → a Xᵣ,ₛ b

The stack symbol T must be the same on the push and pop. Between them, Xᵣ,ₛ generates a run that leaves T and all symbols below it untouched. That middle segment can itself push and pop other symbols.

The labels a and b each stand for either one input terminal or ε. If a is ε, omit it from the right-hand side. If b is ε, omit it. If both are ε, the rule is Xₚ,ᵩ → Xᵣ,ₛ. There is no literal ε token to read.

For normalized machines these three families cover every balanced run: it is empty; it returns to the starting height before its end and can be split; or its first pushed symbol is popped only at the end, enclosing one smaller balanced segment.

sections.title: What the proof establishes
sections.html:
For soundness, show that every grammar rule describes a legal machine segment. Empty segments, concatenated segments, and a correctly matched push/pop pair are all legal. An induction on a parse tree then shows that every terminal string generated by Xₚ,ᵩ has the promised machine run.

For completeness, take a balanced machine run. If it is empty, use the empty rule. Otherwise inspect its stack heights. Split it at an intermediate return to the starting height if one exists. If none exists, match its first push to its last pop. Apply the corresponding rule and recurse on shorter segments. Thus every accepting run has a derivation.

The point is the meaning assigned to each variable. You do not need to memorize a long list of productions without knowing which computation each one describes.

Here, “induction on a parse tree” means checking the empty base segment, then showing that if the child subtrees describe valid smaller segments, the parent rule combines them into the promised larger segment. Repeating that reasoning reaches the start variable.

Use the following exact four-edge machine. It starts in p, accepts only in f, and has empty stack at the beginning and end of its accepting run. No normalization is needed for this example.

Xₚ,ₛ → a Xᵣ,ᵣ b
Xₛ,𝒻 → c Xₜ,ₜ d
Xᵣ,ᵣ → ε

These are the useful rules for the example. The generic construction also adds other state-pair variables and rules; unused or unproductive ones can be removed afterward.

We now explain the useful grammar rules above, one computation segment at a time.

steps.title: Choose the start variable
steps.html: The machine starts at p and accepts only at f. Write Start → Xₚ,𝒻. This variable must describe a complete empty-to-empty run.

steps.title: Split where the stack first returns to empty
steps.html: After reading ab, the machine is in s with empty stack. Use Xₚ,𝒻 → Xₚ,ₛ Xₛ,𝒻. The shared state s is necessary; arbitrary incompatible endpoints would not form a run.

steps.title: Convert the A push/pop pair
steps.html: The a-edge pushes A and enters r. The b-edge leaves r and pops that same A. Therefore Xₚ,ₛ → a Xᵣ,ᵣ b. There is no intervening move, so Xᵣ,ᵣ → ε. This segment generates ab.

steps.title: Convert the B push/pop pair
steps.html: The c-edge pushes B and enters t. The d-edge leaves t and pops B. Add Xₛ,𝒻 → c Xₜ,ₜ d and Xₜ,ₜ → ε. This segment generates cd.

steps.title: Finish and compare the languages

practice.hint: Compare the pushed and popped stack symbols, not just the state names.
practice.solution: No. The outer stack symbol must match: the symbol pushed at the beginning must be the one popped at the end. A middle balanced segment leaves that outer symbol untouched. A push of A and pop of B do not form a matching pair.

practice.prompt: A p→r transition consumes ε and pushes T. An s→q transition reads b and pops T. Write the matching-pair production.
practice.hint: The first edge contributes no input terminal.
practice.solution: Write Xₚ,ᵩ → Xᵣ,ₛ b. The ε label does not appear as a literal terminal. The inside variable still has indices r and s, the states immediately after the push and immediately before the matching pop.

practice.prompt: Why does Xₚ,ᵩ → Xₚ,ᵣXₜ,ᵩ fail as a generic concatenation rule when r≠t?
practice.hint: The end state of one run must be the start state of the next.
practice.solution: The first variable ends in r but the next starts in t. There need not be any machine transition connecting them. Correct concatenation uses the same middle state: Xₚ,ᵩ → Xₚ,ᵣXᵣ,ᵩ.

check.prompt: What is the meaning of Xₚ,ᵩ in the state-pair construction?
check.answer: It generates the inputs of runs from p to q that start and end at the same stack height without popping below that height.
check.explanation: With an empty starting stack this means an empty-to-empty run. The untouched stack suffix interpretation allows the variable to describe a nested segment.

transfer.prompt: A normalized machine has p --read a, push A→ r, r --read b, push B→ s, s --read c, pop B→ t, and t --read d, pop A→ f. It has no other transitions. Build the useful grammar rules and derive its accepted string.

Then Start ⇒ Xₚ,𝒻 ⇒ aXᵣ,ₜd ⇒ abXₛ,ₛcd ⇒ abcd. Unlike the opening example, this run is nested: the stack does not return to empty halfway through.

setup:
Lessons 17–18 turned a grammar into a machine. We now go in the other direction: describe complete pieces of a PDA run with grammar variables.

Xₚ,ᵩ is one variable indexed by two states. Read it as “a balanced run from state p to state q.” Balanced means it restores the starting stack height and never removes the stack below that height. The subscripts are state names, not characters to generate.

The small example starts with an empty stack and accepts only in its specified final state f after all input is consumed and the stack is empty. An empty stack in the initial nonfinal state does not accept ε. This is a different declared convention from ordinary empty-stack acceptance in lesson 10. Its transitions only push one symbol or pop one symbol; the longer conversion explains how to prepare other machines.
bridge: The conversion proves that PDA languages are context-free. It does not preserve or establish determinism; lesson 20 separates those claims.

title: Check determinism and its limits
summary: Distinguish one enabled next move from a successful nondeterministic choice, and declare the acceptance convention.
goals: Check a PDA for overlapping choices, including epsilon versus input transitions.
Explain why a visible middle marker permits deterministic stack matching.
State the standard empty-stack DPDA caveat and use an end marker correctly.

sections.title: Begin with two nearly identical language problems
sections.html:
Compare {w#wᴿ : w ∈ {a,b}*} and {wwᴿ : w ∈ {a,b}*}. Here wᴿ means the reversal of w. The first language contains a visible separator #. The second has no separator.

For a marked input such as ab#ba, push the symbols before #, change phase when # is read, and pop matching symbols afterward. At each step the phase and next input determine what to do. For unmarked input abba, an NPDA can guess where to stop pushing and begin matching. The even-length palindrome language is context-free, but no DPDA recognizes it. The need to guess the middle explains the standard construction; proving that every possible DPDA fails requires a separate theorem.

sections.title: The formal test for a standard DPDA
sections.html:
In the usual model, a transition depends on the state, next input symbol or ε, and current top stack symbol. A DPDA must satisfy both conditions:

  1. For each state q, stack top A, and input choice a or ε, there is at most one possible transition.
  2. If an ε-input transition is enabled for state q and stack top A, then no input-consuming transition may be enabled for that same q and A.

The second rule prevents a choice between “read the next symbol” and “take an ε step first.” An ε transition is not automatically nondeterministic. It is allowed when it has no competing move. Some teaching conventions impose a stricter no-epsilon version; label that extra restriction explicitly.

If your diagram permits “ignore the stack” transitions, check them against every possible stack top. A general transition and a top-specific transition can overlap. Count enabled transitions in a complete configuration, rather than merely counting the arrows drawn from a state.

sections.title: Nondeterministic does not mean random
sections.html:
An NPDA accepts if there exists one finite accepting path. It does not require every path to succeed, and it is not assigned a probability of choosing the right path. A simulator may explore choices one at a time or in parallel; that is an implementation method.

A generic grammar-derived PDA usually has choices such as ε,S/aSb and ε,S/ε at the same stack top S. It is a valid NPDA, even when the grammar’s language has a completely different deterministic recognizer. A nondeterministic construction does not prove the language needs nondeterminism.

Similarly, an unambiguous grammar does not automatically give a DPDA. The grammar S → aSa | bSb | ε is unambiguous for even palindromes, but the unmarked even-palindrome language is not deterministic context-free.

sections.title: Construct the marked palindrome recognizer
sections.html:
Use states push, match, and accept; initial stack marker Z; and final-state acceptance after consuming all input. The top-left stack contains the unmatched prefix in reverse order.

StateInputTopReplacementNext state
pushaT ∈ {a,b,Z}aTpush
pushbT ∈ {a,b,Z}bTpush
push#T ∈ {a,b,Z}Tmatch

The last transition leaves Z in place and enters a final state with no outgoing moves. It has no competing input transition when top is Z, so the machine remains deterministic. If unread input remains after that step, acceptance fails. In particular, a second # is never permitted. The shortest accepted input is #, corresponding to w = ε.

sections.title: Declare what happens when input ends
sections.html:
Under the standard top-symbol DPDA model, an empty stack has no top symbol, so no further move is possible. A language accepted by empty stack must therefore be prefix-free: no accepted string is a proper prefix of another. The unique run cannot empty its stack for a short accepted input and retain symbols to continue on a longer one sharing that prefix.

Balanced brackets are not prefix-free: both [] and [][] are valid. Their ordinary final-state DPDA is therefore not automatically an ordinary empty-stack DPDA. An NPDA may guess when to take an epsilon cleanup.

To finish deterministically, append an explicit right-end marker $ outside the original alphabet. Recognize {w$ : w ∈ L}, popping the bottom marker only when reading $. A simulator’s input-exhaustion test or ability to continue from empty stack is a different convention; declare it.

For an end-marker version of our marked-palindrome recognizer, replace its final transition by read $, pop Z, push ε. Supply ab#ba$ instead of ab#ba.

sections.title: Keep the conclusions at the correct level
sections.html:
ClaimCorrect conclusion
A CFG was converted to a PDAThe language is recognized by an NPDA.
A diagram has two enabled choices in one configurationThat diagram is nondeterministic.
One natural design needs a midpoint guessThat design is nondeterministic; a language-level impossibility still needs a theorem.
A language is recognized by a DPDAIt is a deterministic context-free language, hence context-free.
A language is context-freeIt need not be deterministic context-free.

Supplemental convention checks: Virginia Tech OpenDSA: formal DPDA conditions; Automata Theory and Formal Languages, Theorem 3.3.10 and Fact 3.3.11; Waterloo lecture 11: PDA conventions and deterministic limits.

worked.title: Trace ab#ba and test the deterministic choices
worked.intro:
Target input: ab#ba. Start in push with stack Z, top on the left. Use final-state acceptance, with accept as the only final state and no outgoing transitions from it. The complete table is:

StateInputTopReplacementNext state
pushaT ∈ {a,b,Z}aTpush
pushbT ∈ {a,b,Z}bTpush
push#T ∈ {a,b,Z}Tmatch
matchaaεmatch
matchbbεmatch
matchεZZaccept

There is no added $ in this version. # is the one required input separator; Z remains as the bottom marker when the final state is reached. A row with T represents one row for each T in {a,b,Z}.

steps.title: Read a in push phase
steps.html: Stack Z becomes aZ. The only applicable transition reads a and pushes a above the current top.

steps.title: Read b in push phase
steps.html: Stack aZ becomes baZ. The stack now stores the prefix ab in the reverse order needed for comparison.

steps.title: Read the visible separator
steps.html: On # change from push to match, leaving stack baZ unchanged. There is no guess about where the first half ends.

steps.title: Match b and then a
steps.html: Reading b pops b: baZ → aZ. Reading a pops a: aZ → Z. A mismatch, such as input a while top is b, has no transition.

steps.title: Finish without introducing a competing choice
steps.html: At top Z in match state, the only enabled move is the ε transition to accept. All input has been consumed, so the run accepts. For ab#baa, the same transition would reach accept with a still unread, and the run rejects. For ab#ab, matching fails earlier.

practice.prompt: In state q with top A, one loop reads a and another loop consumes ε. Each has a single destination. Is this deterministic?
practice.hint: Single destinations do not remove the choice between the two loops.
practice.solution: No. With next input a, both the input-reading move and the ε move are enabled. The machine can choose which step to take, violating the DPDA condition. Determinism is about the enabled next action for a complete configuration.

practice.prompt: A state has an ε move only when top is Z. Its input-reading transitions all require top A. Is that fact alone a determinism violation?
practice.hint: Ask whether any one stack top enables both kinds of move.
practice.solution: No. The guards are disjoint: top cannot be A and Z simultaneously. This can be deterministic if every individual case also has at most one destination and no other transition overlaps. An ε transition by itself is allowed in the standard definition.

practice.prompt: Does finding a nondeterministic PDA for {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0} prove the language is not deterministic context-free?
practice.hint: A construction is one recognizer, not a classification of every possible recognizer.
practice.solution: No. A direct deterministic recognizer pushes while reading a, switches on the first b, and pops while reading b, with an appropriate final-state or explicit end-marker convention. The generic grammar-derived machine has choices, but another design can recognize the same language deterministically.

check.prompt: Can every CFL be recognized by some DPDA?
check.answer: No. DPDAs recognize a proper subset of the context-free languages.
check.explanation: The CFG–PDA equivalence theorem uses nondeterministic PDAs. Unmarked even palindromes over a two-symbol alphabet are a standard CFL outside the deterministic subclass.

transfer.prompt: Design the deterministic recognizer for {w#wᴿ : w ∈ {0,1}*}. Test #, 01#10, 01#01, 0##0, and 01#10$. State whether $ is part of your input convention.
transfer.solution: Choose the final-state convention with original alphabet {0,1,#} and bottom marker Z. In push state, read 0 or 1 and push that same symbol; on # switch to match without changing the stack. In match state, read 0 only when top is 0 and pop it; likewise for 1. On top Z take the sole ε move to a final state with no outgoing transitions. Accept # and 01#10. Reject 01#01 for a mismatch, 0##0 for a second separator, and 01#10$ because $ is outside this declared input alphabet. If instead you choose the explicit-endmarker convention, declare alphabet {0,1,#,$}, consume $ only on top Z in match state, and pop Z. Then 01#10$ is accepted and 01#10 without its end marker is incomplete.
