setup:
Lesson 16 used deterministic counting, while lesson 17’s general conversion could branch. Here we distinguish a particular machine being nondeterministic from a whole language requiring nondeterminism.

To check a machine, fix the state and top symbol. Each next input symbol must allow at most one action. If an ε action is available, no input-reading action may compete at that same state and top. ε moves can therefore be deterministic when they are forced.

The worked language has an input separator #, as in ab#ba, and a separate stack marker Z. The separator tells the machine exactly when to stop pushing and begin matching. The example uses final-state acceptance: all input must be consumed, but Z remains. It does not append $ unless that alternative convention is explicitly chosen.
bridge: A particular nondeterministic design does not prove a language impossible for all DPDAs. The next lessons make a stronger negative claim about all CFGs and PDAs, using the CFL pumping lemma.

title: Read the CFL pumping lemma
summary: Read every symbol, identify which choices belong to you, and see why a repeated variable in a parse tree gives two pieces that repeat together.
goals: Read both Greek-letter and Latin-letter versions of the CFL pumping lemma.
Distinguish a necessary property from a method that proves a language is context-free.
Explain all three pumping conditions and the order of choices.
Connect the five string pieces to two repeated nonterminals in a parse tree.

sections.title: Start with one complete example
sections.html:
The grammar S → 0S1 | ε generates {0n1n : n ≥ 0}. One derivation is S ⇒ 0S1 ⇒ 00S11 ⇒ 000111. Repeating the recursive rule adds a 0 on the left and a 1 on the right. Removing one use deletes one of each. The two additions must stay coordinated.

For the particular string 000111, take u = 00, v = 0, x = ε, y = 1, z = 11. Then uvixyiz = 02+i12+i for every integer i ≥ 0. At i = 0 it is 0011; at i = 1 it is the original string; at i = 2 it is 00001111. This is a concrete demonstration, not a claim that every possible split will work.

sections.title: The theorem, written carefully
sections.html:
If L is context-free, there is an integer p ≥ 1 such that every s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p has a decomposition

s = u v x y z
|vxy| ≤ p
|vy| > 0
u vⁱ x yⁱ z ∈ L for every integer i ≥ 0

A decomposition is a division into five consecutive pieces, in the original order. A piece may be empty, but v and y cannot both be empty. In |vy|, the two pieces are concatenated: its length is |v| + |y|. The middle piece x does not repeat.

The pumping window is the consecutive substring vxy. Its entire length, including the unchanged middle x, is at most p. The window may occur anywhere in the string. The condition is not |uv| ≤ p; that would confuse this lemma with the regular-language version.

sections.title: Translate the notation used in the slides
sections.html:
Slide symbolThis lessonRead it as
σsthe complete chosen string
nₗpthe pumping length for the language
α, β, γ, δ, φu, v, x, y, zthe five consecutive string pieces
kithe number of copies of each pumped piece

αβkγδkφ reads: alpha, followed by k copies of beta, followed by gamma, followed by k copies of delta, followed by phi. At k = 0, beta and delta disappear. The same exponent applies to both pieces; you cannot pump one twice and the other three times.

Letters are local variable names. Another book may call the unchanged middle piece w and the final piece y. Identify the positions that carry exponents before doing a calculation.

sections.title: Who controls each choice?
sections.html:
OrderChoiceIn a proof of non-context-freeness
1pThe assumed lemma supplies an arbitrary pumping length. You do not assign p = 3.
2sYou choose a string in L whose length is at least p. It normally depends on p.
3u, v, x, y, zThe assumed lemma may choose any split satisfying the two length conditions. Your proof must cover every such split.
4iYou choose an integer i ≥ 0 that makes the pumped string leave L. Different cases may use different i.

The exact claim you must establish is: for every possible pumping length, there is a suitable string such that every legal split fails for at least one exponent. A single bad split establishes nothing about the other splits. One good exponent also establishes nothing about the requirement that every exponent work.

i = 1 always reproduces s, so it cannot create the contradiction. Try i = 0 to delete pieces and i = 2 to duplicate them.

In logical words, a valid refutation has the order for every p → choose s → for every legal split → choose i. The last choice may depend on the split, but s must have been fixed before the split was considered.

Supplementary example: Cornell’s deliberately incorrect pumping proof shows why defeating one chosen split is insufficient.

sections.title: Why a parse tree supplies five pieces
sections.html:
This section explains why the theorem is true. You may return to it after practising the pumping conditions; the following non-CFL proofs use the theorem, not a calculation of its bound.

A fixed grammar has finitely many variables. A sufficiently long derived string needs a sufficiently deep parse tree because every production has a finite right-hand side. Along a long enough root-to-leaf path, some variable X therefore appears twice.

  1. Choose a parse tree for the string with the fewest nodes.
  2. Find two occurrences of the same variable on one deep path, sufficiently close to the leaves.
  3. The upper X generates vxy. The lower X generates x. Everything before the upper subtree is u, and everything after it is z.
  4. The derivation between the X occurrences has the form X ⇒* vXy. Repeating it adds a copy of v to the left and a copy of y to the right.
  5. Replacing the upper subtree by the lower one produces uxz. Inserting another copy of the upper context produces uvvxyyz.

If v and y were both empty, the smaller subtree would derive exactly the original string using fewer nodes. That contradicts the choice of a smallest tree. Thus |vy| > 0. Choosing the repeated variables near the bottom bounds the size of the upper subtree, giving |vxy| ≤ p.

Optional: one conservative bound from the grammar

For a more explicit bound, let b be the larger of 2 and the maximum number of symbols on a production's right-hand side, and let m be the number of variables. A tree of height h has at most bh terminal leaves. A conservative bound such as p = bm+1 forces a long path; among its last m+1 variable nodes there is a repeated variable. The exact smallest pumping length is not needed in a non-CFL proof.

sections.title: What the lemma can establish
sections.html:
The logical direction is context-free ⇒ has the pumping property. Finding that the pumping property fails proves that a language is not context-free. Finding a split that pumps does not prove context-freeness. To prove a language context-free, construct a correct CFG or PDA, or apply an appropriate closure theorem.

This is also why an unsuccessful pumping attempt is not evidence that the language is context-free. The chosen string or the case analysis may simply be unsuitable.

worked.title: Read and verify a legal pumping split
worked.intro:
Use L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}, generated by S → 0S1 | ε. For the single string 000111, inspect the supplied split:

uvxyz
000ε111

For this demonstration use bound p = 2. We will check the split conditions and the pumped results. This numerical illustration teaches how pumping works; the non-CFL proofs in later lessons keep p arbitrary and do not choose their own split.

steps.title: Write the five pieces
steps.html: Set u = 00, v = 0, x = ε, y = 1, z = 11. Concatenating them gives exactly 000111.

steps.title: Check the window
steps.html: vxy = 01, so |vxy| = 2 ≤ p. Although v and y were separated by x, x is empty here.

steps.title: Check that something changes
steps.html: |vy| = |0| + |1| = 2 > 0. At least one pumped piece is nonempty.

steps.title: Pump down, keep, and pump up
steps.html: i = 0 gives 0011. i = 1 gives 000111. i = 2 gives 00001111. At an arbitrary i the result has 2+i zeros followed by 2+i ones, so it stays in the language.

steps.title: State the precise conclusion
steps.html: This split works for this string. The language is known to be context-free from S → 0S1 | ε. The demonstration explains the lemma; it is not a replacement for the grammar proof.

practice.prompt: For u = a, v = bc, x = d, y = e, z = f, write the original string and the results for i = 0 and i = 2.
practice.hint: Only v and y carry exponents. Preserve the original order.
practice.solution: The original is abcdef. At i = 0, the result is adf. At i = 2, the result is abcbcdeef. The d occurs once in each result because x is unchanged.

practice.prompt: A proof chooses s = aᵖbᵖcᵖ, then announces v = a and y = c. Identify the missing justification.
practice.hint: Can a window of length at most p contain both of these selected characters? Who chooses the split?
practice.solution: The proof has chosen the split instead of treating all legal splits. In fact, for this string, a window containing an a and a c must also include the whole b-block and has length at least p+2. That proposed split is illegal. A correct proof starts with an arbitrary legal split and uses the window bound to restrict its locations.

practice.prompt: Must both pumped pieces be nonempty? Must the unchanged middle piece be nonempty?
practice.hint: Read the condition |vy| > 0 exactly.
practice.solution: No. Either v or y may be empty, but they cannot both be empty. The middle x may also be empty. For example, v = ε, x = ab, y = a satisfies the nonempty-pumped-pieces condition because |vy| = 1.

check.prompt: If one split fails when pumped, have you proved the language is not context-free?
check.answer: No. Every split satisfying the length conditions must fail for some exponent.
check.explanation: The lemma promises the existence of a good split, so a counterproof must eliminate all candidate good splits.

transfer.prompt: Write a six-line non-CFL proof template with spaces for the witness string, window argument, cases, and contradiction.
transfer.solution:
1. Assume L is context-free and let p be its pumping length.
  2. Choose s = … and verify s ∈ L and |s| ≥ p.
  3. Let s = uvxyz be any split with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| > 0.
  4. Use the shape of s and the window bound to describe every possible split.
  5. In each case choose i ≥ 0 and prove uvⁱxyⁱz ∉ L using a specific membership condition.
  6. This contradicts the lemma, so L is not context-free.

setup:
Until now, you established that languages are context-free by building grammars or PDAs. We now introduce a way to prove that a language is not context-free. The pumping lemma says that every sufficiently long string in a CFL has some pair of coordinated pieces that can repeat or disappear while staying in the language.

Pieces in s = u v x y zWhat pumping does
u and zKeep the outside prefix and suffix unchanged.
v and yRepeat both using the same exponent i. At i = 0 both disappear; at i = 2 both occur twice.
xKeep this middle piece once. It may be empty.
pA length bound supplied by the assumed theorem. It is not the pumping exponent i.

A decomposition is a split into five consecutive pieces. |vxy| ≤ p bounds their whole consecutive window; |vy| > 0 says at least one repeated piece is nonempty. The worked numerical example explains the operation. In a non-CFL proof, p remains arbitrary and your argument must defeat every legal split.
bridge: Remember the choice order: the lemma supplies p, you choose the witness, the split remains arbitrary, and then you choose a failing exponent. Lesson 22 applies that structure to three equal blocks.

title: Prove three equal blocks are not context-free
summary: Use a bounded pumping window to make an exhaustive proof. Check both the order of symbols and the required equalities.
goals: Choose a witness that lies in the language and depends on the pumping length.
Prove that the pumping window cannot reach three consecutive blocks.
Give a complete non-CFL proof covering empty pieces and boundary-crossing pieces.
Distinguish a count contradiction from an order contradiction.

sections.title: Understand the membership test first
sections.html:
Let L = {anbncn : n ≥ 0}. A string belongs to L exactly when it consists of an a-block, then a b-block, then a c-block, and the three block lengths agree.

StringMember?Reason
εYesn = 0
abcYesn = 1
aabbccYesn = 2
aabbbccNounequal block lengths
ababccNothe symbol order is wrong

The intuitive difficulty is that one count must be checked twice in sequence. That observation helps select a proof, but it does not prove impossibility: a formal proof must rule out every possible CFG or PDA. The pumping lemma gives that conclusion.

sections.title: The bounded-window observation
sections.html:
Assume a pumping length p and choose s = apbpcp. The middle b-block already has p symbols. A substring that contains an a and a c must contain that whole b-block plus at least one a and one c. Its length is at least p+2.

Therefore the window vxy, whose length is at most p, cannot contain both an a and a c. It lies within one block or crosses one adjacent boundary. The pumped pieces v and y lie inside that same window, so together they can alter at most two of the three symbol counts. At least one count stays at p.

This is about consecutive positions, not merely the number of symbols that repeat. Even if v and y are very short, the unchanged x between them contributes to the window length.

sections.title: The shortest complete argument: delete the pieces
sections.html:
Choose i = 0. The pumped string is uxz. Deletion preserves the a-before-b-before-c order. Because |vy| > 0, at least one of the three symbol counts decreases. Because the window omits either a or c, at least one count remains exactly p. The three counts cannot all be equal, so uxz ∉ L.

This argument covers every legal split at once. It includes v empty, y empty, both nonempty, pieces within one block, and pieces crossing a boundary. A whole block might disappear, but then its count is 0 while an untouched count is p ≥ 1, which still violates equality.

sections.title: The slide-style alternative: duplicate and check cases
sections.html:
You can instead use i = 2. This version makes the distinction between count and order especially clear.

  1. Neither nonempty pumped piece mixes symbol types. Each such piece contains only a's, only b's, or only c's. Duplicating v and y changes at most two counts, changes at least one, and leaves at least one at p. Equal counts are impossible.
  2. A pumped piece contains two symbol types. For example, if it contains arbt with r,t > 0, duplicating it introduces …btar…. An a now occurs after a b. The result is outside a*b*c*, regardless of its counts. A piece containing b's followed by c's fails for the same reason.

A pumped piece cannot contain all three types because it is part of vxy, and the window cannot contain both a and c. These two cases are exhaustive. Do not assume that one pumped piece sits in the a-block and the other in the c-block: the window bound rules that out.

sections.title: Write the final proof in connected sentences
sections.html:
Suppose L were context-free and let p ≥ 1 be its pumping length. Set s = apbpcp. Then s ∈ L and |s| = 3p ≥ p. Consider any decomposition s = uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| > 0. A substring containing both an a and a c has length at least p+2, so vxy omits at least one of these types. Pumping down to uxz therefore leaves one symbol count equal to p, while the nonempty vy causes at least one count to become smaller than p. Thus uxz has unequal counts and is not in L. This contradicts the pumping lemma's requirement at i = 0. Consequently L is not context-free.

The proof uses p symbolically. A numerical illustration can make the reasoning easier to inspect, but it cannot replace the arbitrary-p argument.

worked.title: Inspect the proof on aaabbbccc
worked.intro:
Target language: {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Use aaabbbccc and p = 3 to illustrate how the window bound works. A legal split has s = uvxyz, |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| > 0.

At i = 0, delete v and y. At i = 2, repeat each twice. The general proof is independent of these numerical examples: some count must change while another stays p.

steps.title: Choose a witness inside the language
steps.html: aaabbbccc has three of each symbol, in the required order. Its length is 9, at least p.

steps.title: Locate every possible kind of window
steps.html: A window of length at most 3 can be within aaa, bbb, or ccc, or cross the a/b boundary, or cross the b/c boundary. It cannot reach an a and a c because even the shortest such substring is abbbc, of length 5.

steps.title: Try a split crossing a boundary
steps.html: For illustration choose u = aa, v = a, x = b, y = b, z = bccc. Then vxy is abb of length 3. Pumping down gives aabbccc, with counts 2,2,3.

steps.title: Check a mixed pumped piece
steps.html: Another legal split has u = aa, v = ab, x = ε, y = ε, z = bbccc. Pumping up repeats ab and gives aaababbbccc, which has an a after a b. Pumping down also works: it gives aabbccc.

steps.title: Return to all splits
steps.html: The particular examples are not the proof. The general argument is that deletion changes at least one count while some count remains p. Every legal split has those two properties.

practice.prompt: Why is s = aᵖbᵖ a bad witness for proving {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0} non-context-free?
practice.hint: Check membership before checking length.
practice.solution: For p ≥ 1, the proposed string has no c's and has p a's and p b's. It is not in the language, so the assumed pumping lemma imposes no condition on it. Use a witness such as apbpcp.

practice.prompt: Give a complete proof that {0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not context-free.
practice.hint: Renaming the alphabet does not change the window argument.
practice.solution: Assume context-freeness and let p be the pumping length. Choose s = 0p1p2p. It lies in the language and has length 3p. In any legal split, vxy cannot contain both 0 and 2 because that would require at least p+2 symbols. Thus pumping down deletes at least one symbol but leaves one entire symbol count equal to p. The resulting three counts are unequal. This contradicts the pumping property at i = 0, so the language is not context-free.

practice.prompt: A learner says: “v and y together have at most p symbols, so they cannot touch all three blocks.” Is that enough?
practice.hint: What about a short v near the start and a short y near the end?
practice.solution: No. A bound on |vy| alone does not bound how far apart the pieces occur. The actual lemma bounds |vxy|, which includes all intervening symbols in x. That consecutive-window bound is what prevents reaching the first and third blocks.

check.prompt: Why does pumping down necessarily change at least one count?
check.answer: Because |vy| > 0, so deleting v and y removes at least one terminal.
check.explanation: At least one changed count plus at least one untouched count disproves the required equality of all three.

transfer.prompt: Prove {aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not context-free. State exactly why your cases are exhaustive.
transfer.solution: Assume it is context-free and let p be its pumping length. Choose s = apbpcpdp. It belongs to the language and is long enough. A window of length at most p cannot touch three blocks: reaching the first and third of any three consecutive blocks needs the p-symbol middle block plus two endpoint symbols. Therefore every legal split has v and y affecting at most two symbol types. Pumping down changes at least one count, while at least two counts stay p. The four counts are unequal, so the pumped string is outside the language. This contradicts the lemma. The one-window argument covers every possible location and does not assume either pumped piece is nonempty individually.

setup:
Lesson 21 supplied the proof structure. Here the target is L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}: three ordered blocks whose lengths all agree. We assume a pumping length p and choose aᵖbᵖcᵖ, which is a member of length 3p.

The key observation is about a consecutive window. To include an a and a c, it must cross all p bs plus those two endpoint symbols, so it has at least p + 2 symbols. A window of length at most p cannot do that. Some symbol count is therefore untouched by pumping.

Pumping down means choosing i = 0 and deleting v and y. It removes at least one symbol but leaves an untouched count at p, so all three counts cannot remain equal. The worked p = 3 illustration makes those facts visible; the full proof later keeps p arbitrary.
bridge: One changed count and one untouched count defeated equality. Lesson 23 shows why changing counts alone is insufficient when the definition allows inequalities.

title: Choose pumping up or down for inequalities
summary: A proof with inequalities may need a different exponent in different cases. Use explicit changes in each count instead of assuming a symmetry.
goals: Turn a language definition with inequalities into exact membership checks.
Choose a witness on the equality boundary.
Use case-dependent exponents without changing the order of quantifiers.
Cover all decompositions, including empty pieces and mixed pieces.

sections.title: The target language and its boundary
sections.html:
Consider L = {arbsct : 0 ≤ r ≤ s ≤ t}. It requires block order and two inequalities: the a-count is at most the b-count, and the b-count is at most the c-count.

aabbbcccc is a member because 2 ≤ 3 ≤ 4. aaabbccc is not because 3 ≤ 2 is false. aabbbcc is not because 3 ≤ 2 is false for the last two counts.

Choose s₀ = apbpcp after assuming a pumping length p. This is a member because p ≤ p ≤ p. Equal counts place both inequalities exactly at their boundary. Increasing an earlier count or decreasing a later count can immediately break the language condition.

sections.title: Why one fixed exponent is not enough for the easiest argument
sections.html:
If the pumped pieces contain only a's, pumping down makes the a-count smaller. That still satisfies a-count ≤ b-count ≤ c-count. Pump up instead to make the a-count too large.

If the pumped pieces contain only c's, pumping up makes the c-count larger. That also preserves the inequalities. Pump down instead to make the c-count too small.

You are allowed to choose the exponent after inspecting a split. The lemma demands that one good split work for all exponents. To refute it, each split only needs one exponent that fails. The same exponent need not defeat every split.

sections.title: Record what the pumped pieces contain
sections.html:
Let dₐ = |vy|ₐ, dᵦ = |vy|ᵦ, and d𝒸 = |vy|𝒸. These are the numbers of a's, b's, and c's in the two pumped pieces combined. They are nonnegative integers and dₐ + dᵦ + d𝒸 > 0.

At exponent i, the total counts are

a-count = p + (i−1)dₐ
b-count = p + (i−1)dᵦ
c-count = p + (i−1)d𝒸

This count formula is valid even when a pumped piece mixes symbol types. Repetition may also break block order; a violated count inequality is already enough to prove nonmembership.

The bound |vxy| ≤ p means vxy cannot contain both a and c. Consequently dₐ = 0 or d𝒸 = 0, possibly both. This gives a complete two-case analysis.

sections.title: Case 1: no a is pumped
sections.html:
Suppose dₐ = 0. Choose i = 0. The a-count stays p.

  • If dᵦ > 0, the b-count becomes p−dᵦ < p. Then a-count is greater than b-count, violating the first inequality.
  • If dᵦ = 0, nonemptiness forces d𝒸 > 0. The b-count stays p while the c-count becomes smaller than p. The second inequality fails.

We do not claim that both b and c must decrease. One may be unchanged. The two subcases explain exactly which inequality fails.

sections.title: Case 2: at least one a is pumped
sections.html:
Suppose dₐ > 0. The window restriction forces d𝒸 = 0. Choose i = 2. The c-count stays p.

  • If dᵦ > 0, the b-count becomes p+dᵦ > p, so b-count exceeds c-count.
  • If dᵦ = 0, the b-count stays p and the a-count becomes p+dₐ > p, so a-count exceeds b-count.

Again one of the required inequalities fails. If repeating a mixed piece also disrupts block order, that gives an additional reason to reject the string.

The cases dₐ = 0 and dₐ > 0 cover all possibilities. Both lead to a contradiction. Therefore L is not context-free.

sections.title: Relate this to the pure-piece and mixed-piece case method
sections.html:
Another valid organization first asks whether v or y contains two symbol types. A mixed piece can be pumped up to create an earlier symbol after a later one, breaking a*b*c*. If both nonempty pieces are pure, inspect which types are absent and choose up or down accordingly.

The count-change method above is shorter because it also works for mixed pieces. Both methods use the same essential facts: the witness has equal block lengths, the window cannot reach all three blocks, and at least one pumped piece changes something. Whichever method you choose, say which inequality or order condition fails; “the counts change” alone does not imply a contradiction for a language defined by inequalities.

worked.title: Write the entire chained-inequality proof
worked.intro:
Prove that L = {aʳbˢcᵗ : 0 ≤ r ≤ s ≤ t} is not context-free. Use the witness s₀ = aᵖbᵖcᵖ. The complete choice rule is:

Case for the arbitrary legal splitExponentReason a required inequality fails
No a occurs in v or y: dₐ = 0.i = 0: pump down.Either b decreases below unchanged a, or only c decreases below unchanged b.
Some a occurs in v or y: dₐ > 0.i = 2: pump up.No c can be in that short window. Either b rises above unchanged c, or only a rises above unchanged b.

The counts dₐ,dᵦ,d𝒸 refer only to v and y together, not the full window vxy. The steps now turn this case plan into a complete quantified proof.

steps.title: Assume context-freeness
steps.html: Suppose L is context-free. Let p ≥ 1 be the pumping length supplied by the CFL pumping lemma.

steps.title: Choose and validate the witness
steps.html: Let s₀ = apbpcp. The inequalities p ≤ p ≤ p hold, and |s₀| = 3p ≥ p, so the lemma applies.

steps.title: Keep the split arbitrary
steps.html: Let s₀ = uvxyz be any split with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| > 0. Define dₐ,dᵦ,d𝒸 as the combined counts in v and y. A window reaching an a and a c would have at least p+2 characters, so dₐ and d𝒸 cannot both be positive.

steps.title: Handle the no-a case
steps.html: If dₐ = 0, pump down. If dᵦ > 0, the first inequality fails; otherwise d𝒸 > 0 and the second fails. Thus uxz ∉ L.

steps.title: Handle the some-a case
steps.html: If dₐ > 0, d𝒸 = 0. Pump up. If dᵦ > 0, the second inequality fails; otherwise the first fails. Thus uv²xy²z ∉ L.

steps.title: Close the quantified argument
steps.html: Every legal split falls into one case and has an exponent that produces a string outside L. This contradicts the existence of a split that works for every exponent. L is not context-free.

practice.prompt: With p = 4 and pumped-piece counts dₐ = 0, dᵦ = 0, d𝒸 = 2, choose an exponent and identify the exact failed inequality.
practice.hint: Keep the first two counts at 4.
practice.solution: Choose i = 0. The counts become 4,4,2. The condition b-count ≤ c-count fails because 4 ≤ 2 is false. Choosing i = 2 would give 4,4,6 and would not provide a count contradiction.

practice.prompt: With p = 5 and dₐ = 2, dᵦ = 1, d𝒸 = 0, what does pumping up prove?
practice.hint: Compute all three counts before naming the failed inequality.
practice.solution: At i = 2 the counts are 7,6,5. Both inequalities fail: 7 ≤ 6 is false and 6 ≤ 5 is false. One failure is enough. The proof should not merely report that the counts differ, since unequal counts can be allowed by this language.

practice.prompt: A proposed proof uses “without loss of generality, the a-count decreases.” Why is that unjustified here?
practice.hint: Do the inequalities treat a,b,c symmetrically?
practice.solution: The roles are asymmetric. Decreasing the a-count can preserve membership, whereas decreasing the c-count can destroy it. You cannot rename a and c while preserving the same language definition. A valid proof handles the positions explicitly or uses the count-change cases above.

check.prompt: May the proof use i = 0 in one case and i = 2 in another?
check.answer: Yes. The exponent is chosen after the split, and each split only needs one failing exponent.
check.explanation: The lemma requires every exponent to work for its promised split; finding any failing exponent refutes that split.

transfer.prompt: Adapt the proof to {aʳbˢcᵗ : r ≥ s ≥ t ≥ 0}. Explain which pump directions reverse.
transfer.solution: Assume a pumping length p and choose aᵖbᵖcᵖ. For any legal split define dₐ,dᵦ,d𝒸 as before; dₐ and d𝒸 cannot both be positive. If dₐ = 0, pump up: if dᵦ > 0 then b-count exceeds unchanged a-count, and if dᵦ = 0 then d𝒸 > 0 makes c-count exceed unchanged b-count. If dₐ > 0, d𝒸 = 0; pump down: if dᵦ > 0 then b-count falls below unchanged c-count, and otherwise a-count falls below unchanged b-count. Every split fails for an exponent, contradicting the lemma. The language is not context-free.

setup:
Lesson 22 could defeat every split by deleting its pumped pieces. With inequalities, deletion can preserve membership. We must calculate which required inequality fails.

The target is {aʳbˢcᵗ : 0 ≤ r ≤ s ≤ t}. The letters r, s and t count the three blocks. We call the complete witness s₀ to distinguish it from the middle block count s. Use s₀ = aᵖbᵖcᵖ so both inequalities begin at equality.

dₐ, dᵦ, d𝒸 count the as, bs and cs contained in v and y together. Pumping with exponent i changes an original count p to p + (i−1)d: subtract d at i = 0, keep p at i = 1, add d at i = 2. The window bound still prevents pumping both a and c. We choose the exponent after seeing which case the arbitrary split belongs to.
bridge: Name the exact failed condition and keep the split arbitrary. Lesson 24 applies the same discipline when membership requires identical halves rather than only a count relationship.

title: Prove the copy language is not context-free
summary: Finish with a direct pumping proof that identical halves cannot be enforced, then choose between construction, simulation, and impossibility proofs on new problems.
goals: Distinguish identical copying from reversal and from equal total counts.
Prove non-context-freeness of the binary copy language without assuming the midpoint stays fixed.
Use a regular-language intersection correctly as an optional proof tool.
Choose a suitable method and explain the invariant or contradiction independently.

sections.title: Copying is a position-by-position requirement
sections.html:
The copy language is C = {ww : w ∈ {0,1}*}. A member consists of two identical consecutive halves. Examples are ε, 00, 11, 0101, and 001001. The string 0110 is not a member: its halves are 01 and 10.

This differs from {wwR}, where the second half is reversed. A stack naturally retrieves the last stored symbol first, which supports reversal. For C, a pumping proof establishes that no different CFG or PDA construction can circumvent the difficulty.

Even total counts are only a necessary condition for copying. For example, 00111100 contains four 0's and four 1's but has unequal halves 0011 and 1100. A proof must check the required structure, not just parity.

sections.title: Choose blocks longer than the pumping window
sections.html:
Assume C is context-free with pumping length p ≥ 1. Let N = 2p and choose

s = 0ᴺ 1ᴺ 0ᴺ 1ᴺ = (0ᴺ1ᴺ)(0ᴺ1ᴺ).

This is in C, and its length is 4N = 8p ≥ p. The extra block length is deliberate. Pumping down deletes at most p characters, while each block has 2p. No block can disappear. After deleting v and y the string therefore still has exactly four nonempty runs, in the order 0,1,0,1.

The shorter choice 0p1p0p1p also works, but its proof must separately handle a block that is deleted entirely. Using 2p avoids that extra case without changing the method.

sections.title: First prove a small fact about four runs
sections.html:
A run is a maximal consecutive group of equal symbols. If a string has the form 0A1B0D1E with all four exponents positive, then it is a square ww exactly when A = D and B = E.

The reverse direction is immediate: equal pairs give (0A1B)(0A1B). For the forward direction, suppose it is ww. The half w begins in 0 and ends in 1, since the full string does. Let t be the number of changes between adjacent symbols inside w. Since w begins and ends differently, t ≥ 1. The full string ww has 2t+1 changes: t in each copy and one from the final 1 of the first copy to the initial 0 of the second. Our four-run string has exactly three changes, so 2t+1 = 3 and t = 1. Thus w itself must be one nonempty 0-run followed by one nonempty 1-run. The two 0-run lengths agree, and the two 1-run lengths agree.

This fact checks the actual midpoint of any proposed square. It avoids the unjustified claim that pumping leaves the original midpoint in the same position.

sections.title: Use the window to defeat every split
sections.html:
Let s = uvxyz be any decomposition with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| > 0. The window can touch at most two adjacent runs. Reaching two nonadjacent runs would require crossing the full intervening run of length N = 2p, plus one symbol at each endpoint, exceeding p.

Let e₁,e₂,e₃,e₄ count the symbols deleted from each of the four runs by pumping down. Then each e is nonnegative, their sum is between 1 and p, and all positive e values occur in at most two adjacent positions. The pumped-down string is

u x z = 0^(N−e₁) 1^(N−e₂) 0^(N−e₃) 1^(N−e₄).

Each exponent is at least N−p = p > 0. If this string were a square, the four-run fact would require e₁ = e₃ and e₂ = e₄. But the window cannot touch both run 1 and run 3, or both run 2 and run 4. In each pair at least one e is zero. Equal pairs would therefore force all four e values to be zero, contradicting their positive sum.

Thus uxz ∉ C for every legal split. Taking i = 0 contradicts the pumping lemma. Therefore the binary copy language is not context-free.

sections.title: Optional extension: filtering by a regular language
sections.html:
Optional extension. An intersection L ∩ R contains strings belonging to both languages. A language class is closed under an operation when applying that operation keeps you in the class. In the regular-expression filter 0+1+0+1+ below, + means “one or more copies,” not arithmetic addition.

Context-free languages are closed under intersection with a regular language. A PDA can track the finite-state machine for the regular condition alongside its own state without adding another stack. Therefore, if L were context-free and R were regular, L ∩ R would be context-free.

For copying, the regular filter R = 0+1+0+1+ keeps exactly four nonempty runs. The four-run fact shows

C ∩ R = {0ᴬ1ᴮ0ᴬ1ᴮ : A ≥ 1, B ≥ 1}.

The same bounded-window proof shows that this intersection is not context-free, so closure gives another route to the conclusion about C. A proof requested specifically by the pumping lemma can instead use the direct proof above; it already rules out membership in C.

Do not replace R by an arbitrary context-free language and assume the same closure rule. CFLs are not closed under general intersection. For example, the CFLs {arbrct} and {arbscs} intersect in {anbncn}, which you proved non-context-free.

worked.title: A direct copy-language proof you can reconstruct
worked.intro:
Target: C = {ww : w ∈ {0,1}*}. Assume a pumping length p, set N = 2p, and choose s = 0ᴺ1ᴺ0ᴺ1ᴺ. It is the copy of 0ᴺ1ᴺ.

We use the four-run fact explained in the setup: a string 0ᴬ1ᴮ0ᴰ1ᴱ with all four runs nonempty is a copy only when A = D and B = E. Pumping down deletes at least one but at most p symbols in at most two adjacent runs. No run disappears, and a changed run’s matching partner stays unchanged. The steps justify each part of that argument.

steps.title: Make the assumption and pick the witness
steps.html: Assume C is context-free and take its pumping length p. Choose s = (02p12p)(02p12p). State explicitly why this is a copy and why it is long enough.

steps.title: Keep the decomposition arbitrary
steps.html: For any legal split, vxy has length at most p. All deleted symbols therefore lie in at most two adjacent runs. At least one symbol is deleted because |vy| > 0.

steps.title: Preserve all four runs
steps.html: Deleting at most p symbols from a run of length 2p leaves at least p symbols. So the pumped result still has four nonempty runs. This is why the witness uses 2p rather than p in each block.

steps.title: Apply the square criterion
steps.html: A four-run string 0A1B0D1E can be a square only if A = D and B = E. Justify this with the three-change argument; do not simply assume the split stays at the original boundary.

steps.title: Find a changed run with an unchanged partner
steps.html: Some run loses at least one symbol. Its matching partner, two runs away, cannot be touched by the same bounded window. The changed run has length below 2p while its partner still has length 2p, violating one of the required equalities.

steps.title: Conclude for every split
steps.html: Thus pumping down always leaves C. That contradicts the lemma at i = 0, so C is not context-free. The proof covers windows in either original half and windows crossing their boundary.

practice.prompt: For p = 4, take s = 0⁸1⁸0⁸1⁸. Suppose pumping down deletes two symbols from run 2 and two from run 3. Why is the result not a copy, even though the total counts of both symbols are even?
practice.hint: Compute all four run lengths, then use the four-run square criterion.
practice.solution: The result is 08160618. It contains 14 zeros and 14 ones, so parity alone does not reject it. Run 1 and run 3 have different lengths, as do run 2 and run 4. By the four-run square criterion it cannot have identical halves. The four deleted symbols fit in a length-4 window crossing the middle boundary, so this numerical situation respects the window bound.

practice.prompt: Why is “only the first half changes, so the halves differ” an incomplete pumping argument?
practice.hint: Where is the midpoint of the shorter pumped string?
practice.solution: Deleting symbols changes the total length and can move the midpoint. The new halves need not be the original halves with a local deletion. A complete argument checks the structure at the new midpoint. Here the four-run square criterion does that independently of positions.

practice.prompt: Explain why {wwᴿ : w ∈ {0,1}*} is context-free while {ww : w ∈ {0,1}*} is not.
practice.hint: For the positive claim, supply a grammar. For the negative claim, name the proof you now have.
practice.solution: The grammar S → 0S0 | 1S1 | ε generates exactly even-length binary palindromes, which are the strings wwᴿ. Each recursive step adds matching outer symbols. This proves that language context-free. The direct pumping proof above proves that identical same-order copying ww is not context-free. Do not infer the difference solely from an informal statement about stack order.

check.prompt: In the copy proof, why do we choose each block to have length 2p?
check.answer: Pumping down deletes at most p symbols, so every block stays nonempty and the four-run square criterion remains applicable.
check.explanation: A longer legal witness simplifies the exhaustive proof; the lemma only requires its length to be at least p.

Core proof. Suppose D is context-free and let p ≥ 1 be its pumping length. Put N = 2p and choose s = aᴺbᴺaᴺbᴺ. This is the copy of aᴺbᴺ, so s ∈ D, and |s| = 8p ≥ p.

The four-run criterion checks the actual new halves without keeping the old midpoint fixed.

This works for every legal split and contradicts the lemma’s requirement at i = 0. Therefore D is not context-free.

setup:
Lesson 6 generated a word followed by its reversal. Here we test same-order copying, C = {ww : w ∈ {0,1}*}. For w = 01, copying gives 0101 and reversal gives 0110. Counting totals is not enough to tell them apart.

A run is a maximal consecutive group of the same symbol. The witness 0ᴺ1ᴺ0ᴺ1ᴺ has four nonempty runs. Choose N = 2p; deleting at most p symbols cannot erase any run.

We need this four-run fact before using it: 0ᴬ1ᴮ0ᴰ1ᴱ, with all exponents positive, is a copy exactly when A = D and B = E. To see why, a proposed half begins in 0 and ends in 1. If it has t internal symbol changes, two identical halves have 2t + 1 changes in total, including their join. Four runs mean three changes, so t = 1. Each half is therefore one 0-run followed by one 1-run, and the corresponding lengths agree.

The proof uses that fact to check the actual halves after deletion; it does not assume the old midpoint stays fixed. The regular-language intersection argument later on is optional.
